news.title: Won historic races, flipped seats from Republicans to Democrats: US Congresswoman hails two Indian-American winners
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 11 (IANS) Two newly elected Indian-American lawmakers have secured hard-fought victories in US Congressional races and are preparing to enter the House of Representatives, a development Congresswoman Grace Meng says reflects the community's growing place in American political life. In an exclusive interview with IANS, the New York Democrat welcomed the election of Pia Dandiya and Dr Amish Shah, saying their victories came after difficult contests in which Republicans had invested heavily. Meng said she had been in contact with both candidates throughout their campaigns and had met them in Washington as they attended orientation for incoming members of Congress. "There was a lot of money put against them," she said, referring to Republican campaign efforts. "Not only did they win historic races," she said, adding that "they flipped seats from the Republican Party to the Democrats." Her comments underlined the significance she attached to the candidates' success beyond their individual victories. Both will arrive on Capitol Hill as members of a new Congress in which Democrats expect to hold the majority. Meng said the candidates had faced difficult races, rather than straightforward contests, and highlighted both their personal accomplishments and the challenges of securing a place in Congress. Describing their credentials, she said "they are accomplished people in their own right" and noted that they were now entering Congress. The Congresswoman said she had followed their campaigns closely and remained in contact with them as they moved towards taking office. "I saw them again this morning," she said, recalling her meeting with the incoming lawmakers in Washington. She compared the orientation process to the start of a new school, as newly elected representatives learn their way around Congress and prepare for the responsibilities ahead. Meng said the newcomers were settling in well. The victories, she suggested, were part of a broader change in the visibility and participation of Indian Americans in the United States. "But it just shows that the Indian American community is becoming more and more a part of the fabric of our American society," she said. Meng said elected representatives from the community would work on a broad range of national issues, rather than issues affecting Indian Americans alone. Her remarks placed the two newcomers in a wider picture of political participation, from campaigns and legislative work to representation at the highest levels of government. She pointed to the political prominence of former Vice President Kamala Harris, whose mother was from India, as an example of Indian-American participation in senior public office. "Indian Americans have made great strides," she said. Asked what Democratic control of Congress could mean for the community, Meng expressed hope that lawmakers would find common ground and help Indian Americans feel included. The Congresswoman did not outline an agenda for either new representative. Instead, she emphasised that both had earned their places through demanding contests and would now join colleagues working on legislation across a range of subjects. The two incoming representatives won different kinds of contests on November 3. Shah, a physician and former Arizona state legislator, defeated Republican Jay Feely in Arizona's 1st Congressional District, a seat previously held by Republican David Schweikert, who did not seek re-election. Dandiya, a former school principal, defeated Republican Casey Askar in Florida's 22nd Congressional District.

news.title: Obsolete And Overdue: Withdrawing US Forces From The Gulf
news.text:
Presumptions of friendship and guarantees in
international relations are never secure and rarely lasting.
Even when they are given the stamp of firm endurance, a
closer look will find greater benefits accruing to one party
over the other. When one needs to persuade a weaker power
into surrendering real estate and valuable terrain for the
more powerful counterpart to use, always employ the
terminology of “joint-facility”, “joint-operations”
or some such. That will go a long way into validating the
mendacity of an arrangement.

The Gulf Arab states are
the latest to learn this lesson from the United States,
whose guardianship credentials have been looking
particularly shabby of late. Having not sought the conflict
with Iran that the US, in collusion with Israel, started at
the end of February, they now face the prospect of a
diminished American presence once hostilities with Tehran

For decades, the Gulf Cooperation Council states
sought to create a defence order based on gluttonous arms
purchases and extensive offerings to US military personnel
in terms of bases and facilities, the assumption being that
this would guarantee them against attack. While the
presumptive attacker in that case was Iran, the GCC states
did not spare diplomacy in attempting to mollify Tehran,
adopting a conscious
policy of distancing from US-Israeli policy. The
presence of US forces, in offering that insurance of
security, also encouraged those in the Gulf region to
advertise grandly as destinations for stable investment,
capital and labour (however shoddy the conditions),
sheltered by the comforts of the US imperial

The American promissory note guaranteeing Gulf
security was spectacularly invalidated in the opening days
of March. Shortly after the first US-Israeli strikes hit
Iranian soil, retaliation from Tehran came in an expansive
spray of attacks on GCC states. These caused fires in the
vicinity of luxury accommodation in Dubai. Kuwait’s
international airport was disrupted. The Aramco facility in
Ras Tanura, responsible for the production of more than
half-a-million barrels of oil per day, was targeted
and damaged. As the strikes continued, it also became clear
that the exorbitantly priced defences long marshalled by the
states came to very little. Sophisticated anti-missile
technology, for instance, could barely account for swift,
stealthy drones of cheaper make yet devastating effect. By
mid-July, the US itself had used up over 1,700 Patriot
interceptors and over 200 THAAD missiles in the Middle

The debate among the policy wonks and wags is
that American influence in the region has not only received
a bruising, but a bruising with consequence. “For the
first time since the great powers dismembered the Ottoman
empire a century ago,” declares
The Economist with haughty certitude, “the Middle
East’s overarching order will no longer be imposed from
afar.” American attempts to shape the region had “run
their course.” As with previous powers – Britain,
France, Russia – the US would still be involved in so far
as its interests demanded it. Force and interventions were
not to be permanently shelved. “But it will abandon its
role as architect.”

The pages of Foreign
Affairs are also filled with the symptoms of imminent
troop withdrawal. Dana Stroul, former Deputy Assistant
Secretary of Defense for the Middle East in the Biden
administration, suggests
moving US forces (the stock weasel word is always
“redeployment”) away from the Persian Gulf. Michael
Fuchs, former Special Assistant to President Joe Biden and
former Deputy Chief of Staff to Vice President Kamala Harris
is even more blunt in light of the “failed Iran War”,
suggesting it to be a “spur for a long-overdue
withdrawal.”

The debate favouring withdrawal from
the Gulf has gathered such momentum as to worry the coterie
of jodhpur imperialists who still insist on the sacrosanct
role of US power. F. Gregory Gause III of Texas A&M
University is almost panicked by this outbreak of Middle
East retreatism, proposing
that “a better option would be a prudent reconsideration
of the US basing structure in the Gulf, engaged in jointly
with the Gulf states that continue to want to host and
support the American presence.”

To add formidable
insult to smarting injury, President Donald Trump is also of
the view that the costs of the catastrophe he was
instrumental in unleashing should be covered by regional
allies. Making the absurd claim that Washington protected
these states in the first place, having demonstrably shown
the opposite to be the case, Trump told
CBS News that they “are going to pay us back any and all
costs that we’ve had for the war.” Without the US,
“they would not exist.” Just to add some fiery topping
to the commentary, the president also bracketed Israel in
their company. “Without us, Israel would not

The focus on the part of the Gulf states
will invariably be one of introspection followed by
arrangements for an intra-defence system sharpened by the
lessons of the Iran War. Collaborative associations with
other states – Turkey and Pakistan, for instance – are
bound to become even more attractive (witness Riyadh’s
move in that direction with the Mecca Joint Defence
Agreement), though any military component will be hampered
by a continuing
addiction to American weapons systems that require
continuous technical support and maintenance from
Washington. Then there is the GCC Unified Military Command,
formerly known as the Peninsula Shield Force. Its
effectiveness, always subsidiary given the heavy reliance on
American brawn, may be revisited. To do that, however, the
Gulf states will have to set aside their own grumbling
differences – indeed, a tall order. US power, in the
meantime, will continue to be eclipsed.

Kampmark was a Commonwealth Scholar at Selwyn College,
Cambridge. He currently lectures at RMIT University. Email:
bkampmark@gmail.com

news.title: Move to have Diwali as federal holiday may gain momentum under Democrats: US Congresswoman Meng (IANS Exclusive)
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 11 (IANS) US Congresswoman Grace Meng believes Democratic control of the House and Senate could improve the chances of making Diwali a federal holiday, and says she will renew her legislative effort in the next Congress. In an exclusive interview with IANS, the New York Democrat said recognising the festival would give Americans beyond the communities that celebrate it an opportunity to understand their cultures and traditions. "When people have a day off for a holiday, it's not just about a day off, but it's an opportunity for everyone, even if you don't celebrate those holidays, to learn about the holiday," she said. Meng first introduced her proposal in 2023 and said the present effort marked its second introduction. Asked about the slow progress, she pointed to the time it took to establish Juneteenth as a national holiday and to secure school holidays in New York. "Yeah, holidays take a long time," she said. "But that's why it's more important to persevere." She said Democratic gains in both chambers of Congress might offer "a stronger chance of this becoming law as well." Asked whether she would introduce the measure again in the new Congress, she replied: "Yes, absolutely." Meng said supporters were collecting co-sponsors in the House and hoped to see the proposal introduced in the Senate. She stressed that the effort should attract support across party lines, describing it as a matter of respect and inclusion for growing Asian-American communities. The Congresswoman recalled supporting school holidays for Lunar New Year, Eid and Diwali when she served in the New York State legislature. Those holidays have since become a reality in New York City, she said. She also described her introduction to Diwali through friends while in high school or college. The festival's message of joy and hope had stayed with her, she said, adding that celebrations and greetings from politicians of both parties had made Diwali more visible across the country. But Meng coupled that progress with a warning about increasing hostility towards South Asian communities. "Anti-South Asian hate online has increased about 240 per cent in the last few years," she said. She did not identify the underlying study during the interview. "It comes into our communities and puts people at risk," she said of hateful rhetoric. Meng referred to what she described as a thwarted mass-shooting attempt at an Illinois Hindu temple, where Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi had been worshipping with his family. She also cited racist activists interrupting a Diwali celebration in Washington state while children were performing. The incidents were cited by Meng during the interview and have not been independently verified for this report. The Congresswoman welcomed the election of two Indian-American members of Congress, saying both had won difficult races and flipped seats from Republican to Democratic control. Meng said she had stayed in touch with them throughout their campaigns and met them again during their orientation in Washington. "I saw them again this morning," she said, adding that both were adjusting well to their new responsibilities. She also cited former Vice President Kamala Harris's rise to one of America's highest offices as evidence of Indian Americans' growing presence in public life. Diwali is celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs, Jains and some Buddhists, including across the Indian diaspora in the United States. The festival has gained recognition through local celebrations, official greetings and school observances, but is not currently a US federal holiday. Making it a federal holiday would require legislation to pass Congress and become law.

news.title: Who Is Mississippi Senate Candidate Scott Colom's Wife, Nadia?
news.text: Democrat Scott Colom continues to hold a slight lead over Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's U.S. Senate race, which remains uncalled a week after Election Day due to the slim margin between the two candidates. Colom led Hyde-Smith by 2,575 votes, or 0.3 percentage points, on Tuesday afternoon, despite the state’s conservative lean. The Associated Press reported that 97 percent of the vote had been counted. Southern states, including those that President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024, saw some of the strongest leftward shifts this year amid national dissatisfaction with the Trump administration and high turnout among Black voters. Mississippi was seen as having a Republican lean, but Democrats began to invest in the seat in the latter stages of the campaign. Who Is Nadia Dale Colom? Scott Colom is married to Nadia Dale Colom. The two live in Columbus, Mississippi, and she is from West Point, Mississippi. They have two daughters in elementary school, according to the Mississippi Free Press. She has served as the executive director of the Golden Triangle Boys and Girls Club. She frequently appeared in campaign videos for Scott Colom and has voiced support for her husband’s campaign. She told WKXI-FM, a radio station in Magee, Mississippi, that she believes 2026 was “our moment to show the country that Mississippi does matter.” “We’re not a state to be written off," she said. "We have very valuable people here, with valuable voices, who deserve better representation than we have right now in Washington.” In a video posted on social media, she praised her husband’s “dedication that he brings to his job as D.A. and just the relentless commitment to the community.” Scott Colom thanked his wife for her support in a Facebook post, writing: "My wife Nadia truly never stops campaigning. I couldn’t do this without her." Could Scott Colom Win the Mississippi Senate Race? The race has not yet been called, but Colom has maintained his lead. Mississippi counties have until November 13 to submit their certified results to the secretary of state’s office, meaning the full vote tally should become clearer by then. Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson broke down the remaining ballots late Monday evening. He said that 75 counties have uploaded their unofficial results, while one uploaded official results. There were 2,578 absentee mail-in ballots still out. He said 15,547 affidavit ballots had been processed, with 76 percent accepted. Could There Be a Recount in the Mississippi Senate Race? In many states, such a narrow margin could trigger a recount, but Mississippi does not have a recount procedure. A candidate could challenge the results in court or appeal to the Senate. Michael Morley, the faculty director of Florida State University’s Election Law Center, told Newsweek last week: “Ultimately, at the end of the day, no matter who gets certified as the winner, no matter what a court says about it, the U.S. Constitution says the Senate itself is the ultimate judge. Even if state officials wind up certifying one of the candidates as the winner, the other could ask the Senate to decline the seat to that person.” A FairVote analysis of 7,437 statewide general elections between 2000 and 2025 found that there were 37 recounts. Only three election results were reversed, according to the report. When Was the Last Time Mississippi Elected a Democratic Senator? Mississippi has not elected a Democratic senator since John Stennis in 1982. He retired in 1988, and the seat flipped to Republicans. How Mississippi Became a Midterm Battleground Mississippi is not ordinarily seen as particularly competitive. Trump performed especially well there in 2024, winning 60.9 percent of the vote to former Vice President Kamala Harris’ 38 percent. In 2020, Trump won by 17 points, 58 percent to 41 percent. He carried the state by 18 points in 2016, 58 percent to 40 percent. Republicans also carried the state by 12 points in 2012 and 13 points in 2008. Due to its large Black population, Mississippi has been a high-floor, low-ceiling state for Democrats. The party regularly receives more than 40 percent of the vote in the Magnolia State but has struggled to win a majority due to its intense racial polarization. Amid a favorable environment that saw shifts across the South, Mississippi trended more than 20 points toward Democrats, making a close race for Senate. The race saw some investment from national Democrats, who were encouraged by polling pointing to a closer-than-expected race. A key part of Colom’s success can be attributed to a 28-second ad that brought national attention to his campaign. The ad begins with a snippet of Hyde-Smith saying that consumers “have so many proteins to choose from” amid frustration with beef prices. The ad then cuts to a man, grilling burgers, who says: "Pick another protein? S***, I'd rather pick another senator instead." A woman in a diner says: "Pick another protein? She done lost her damn mind! I'd rather pick another senator." "Pick another protein? What the f***," a woman in a grocery store says. The ad ends with Colom at a dining table. He laughs, then tells voters: "Pick another senator instead." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Mississippi's U.S. Senate race remained uncalled a week after Election Day, as ballots continued to be counted.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: Keisha Lance Bottoms And Jon Ossoff Prove Joint Campaigning Across Race Wins
news.text:
The sweeping Democratic victories across the American South last week have shattered longstanding assumptions about the political viability of Democratic candidates in conservative strongholds. This sudden blue wave has reshaped the electoral map, capturing statehouses and governors’ mansions through a surge of voter turnout that caught many political analysts off guard. 

As the dust continues to settle after these historic midterm outcomes, a distinct commonality has emerged around four politicians with a shared methodology behind a handful of the cycle’s most surprising upsets. 

In Georgia and Texas, the paths of four candidates converged around a deliberate strategy of shared infrastructure, using joint appearances and pooled resources to build power and win their respective elections in states where Republicans had held large majorities for decades. 

In Georgia, the pairing of Jon Ossoff and Keisha Lance Bottoms provides the initial proof that a coordinated approach could help tilt a deeply contested state blue. Rather than running isolated operations that targeted demographics separately, the two candidates unified their ground games and appeared on the trail as a packaged deal. 

This deliberate unity helped Ossoff secure his reelection to the U.S. Senate and helped propel Bottoms to the governor’s mansion as the first woman to govern Georgia and the first Black woman elected governor of any U.S. state. 

Ossoff backed this shared vision with substantial capital, committing more than $3.6 million into the state party’s coordinated campaign coffers. That funding ensured that the organizing staff, voter databases, and field offices serving his federal race matched the ones driving turnout for Bottoms, creating a seamless experience for voters who could now imagine both leaders as part of a unified ticket. 

In Texas, state representative James Talarico and fellow state lawmaker Gina Hinojosa executed a similar strategy by sharing the stage during their critical closing campaign push across major metro hubs in Houston and San Antonio. Running respectively for the U.S. Senate and the governorship, their historic victories broke over three decades of Republican dominance, with Talarico winning a Senate seat and Hinojosa capturing the governor’s mansion to become the first Latina governor in Texas history. 

Their joint appearances presented a visual and strategic alliance that broke down traditional campaign silos. By locking arms on the trail, they signaled to their respective bases that an investment in and vote for one candidate was an investment in and vote for the other. This close coordination allowed them to maximize their reach, combine their volunteer networks, and present a formidable front that resonated with a diverse electorate weary of fragmented political messaging from candidates with a shared party affiliation. 

Former congressman Beto O’Rourke influenced the tandem strategy in Texas, advising Hinojosa during the early planning stages that the state was too vast for a lone candidate to conquer, making a dual approach necessary if she wanted to win. 

By dividing responsibilities, Talarico engaged rural networks through his faith-based messaging, while Hinojosa appealed to suburban women by focusing on public school funding and advocating for a $1,500 corruption tax refund to return hoarded rainy-day reserves to every household in Texas. 

Pairing Black and Latina women with white men has shown to be a successful pairing in corporate America as well. Workplace research proves that Black and Latina women reach higher corporate positions and receive faster promotions when they have white men serving as their professional sponsors. When white leaders use their influence to vouch for Black and Latino counterparts, they are able to rise above traditional corporate gatekeepers and into senior management. 

Data from McKinsey and Company confirms that this type of promotion and co-signing can be a career accelerant for Black and Latina women. When backed by white sponsors, Black women are over 50% more likely to advance into management roles than peers without that executive support. Similarly, corporate studies show that Latina professionals see a sharp increase in promotion outcomes when a white sponsor actively endorses their credentials for executive positions. 

By using their established platforms to validate the candidacies of Black and Latina women, Talarico and Ossoff were part of political partnerships with Bottoms and Hinojosa that functioned in a similar way to secure statewide victories. 

The partnership between Ossoff, a white man, and Bottoms, a Black woman, built upon a powerful precedent we’ve seen before in politics. In the 2020 presidential election, Joe Biden and Kamala Harris demonstrated that the combination of a white man and a Black woman joining political forces could deliver victory. Harris’ presence on the ticket galvanized Black voters in crucial metropolitan hubs, providing the decisive surge that pushed Biden over the top in key battleground states like Georgia, Michigan, and Pennsylvania.

In the 2024 presidential race, the pairing of Kamala Harris leading the ticket as president and Tim Walz in the supporting vice-presidential role proved unsuccessful, exposing a harsh reality that voters are still intent on reserving the highest seat of power for white men. 

Long-standing studies on political stereotypes and social identities prove that voters are more likely to accept Black women as secondary in political pairings, but heavily penalize them and consider them unelectable or overly aggressive when they seek the primary seat of power. 

In order for the Democrats to secure the White House in 2028, they will need to start considering how much of their political heft should be focused on chipping away at these voters’ biases while also identifying similar pairings around the country of multi-ethnic local campaigns they can start supporting.

The wins in Georgia and Texas prove that Black and Latina candidates can win races on a Democratic ticket in highly contested races in conservative strongholds. Their success or failure once they take office will be an important litmus test for voters everywhere. 

The lessons of recent election cycles show that sustainable coalitions across gender and racial lines are an effective strategy. The challenge ahead for the Democratic Party is to move an electorate that readily accepts a Black woman as second-in-command to finally shatter the ultimate glass ceiling and support her at the top of the ticket. 

A Blue Tsunami Is Putting Democratic Leadership To The TestBlack Women Seize Historic Election Wins Across the US
news.summary: Joint campaigning across race and gender lines delivered historic Democratic victories in long-standing conservative strongholds in Georgia and Texas.

news.title: YAF Announces 30-City ‘Freedom Not Socialism’ Push After Youth Vote Shifts Left
news.text:
Young America’s Foundation (YAF) is announcing plans to launch a new initiative aimed at warning young Americans of the dangers of socialism.

The program, called “Freedom Not Socialism,” will bring conservative voices to high schools and colleges in dozens of cities nationwide over the next two years, YAF President and former Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker told Townhall.

“We looked at a mapping of the 30 most liberal, radicalized cities in America, and said over the next two years, we want to get to every one of these cities to bring these special one-day programs where we’re reaching out to young people, and showing them how to fight back against socialism,” Walker said.

The tour will kick off at YAF’s November Freedom Conference on November 12-14 at the group’s Reagan Ranch in Santa Barbara, California, with speakers including former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, U.S. Representative-elect Michael Alfonso, and Walker, before setting out for cities across the country.

“This campaign is about speaking the truth in ways that are powerful and tangible to young people,” Walker said.

The program’s first stop will be in Los Angeles, followed by planned stops including Chicago, Minneapolis, New York City, Portland, San Francisco, and Seattle. Walker said the city programs will initially target high school students but will also include college speaking events.

Regardless of the city, Walker said he hopes to see “packed events.”

“If you get 800 to 1,000 young people in each of these cities, who are now not just inspired, but equipped to go out and make a difference, that’s like a tidal wave of reaching out to other young people in that area,” Walker said.

The announcement of the initiative follows the results of last week’s midterm elections, in which young voters overwhelmingly voted for Democrat candidates. A Tufts University poll found 54 percent of white male voters aged 18 to 29 voted for Democrat candidates, compared with 43 percent for Republicans. In 2024, roughly 63 percent of young men of the same demographic voted for President Trump, and 35 percent voted for Kamala Harris.

Walker attributed some of the shift among young voters to continued frustration with the economy, rather than complete changes in ideology. 

“Two years later, they’re still upset even though things have gotten somewhat better,” Walker said. “They’re still upset. And so now they were willing to give, not just Democrats, but particularly Democratic socialist candidates, a try.”

But Walker said YAF’s new initiative aims to make the case that free-market principles offer a better answer to young voters’ economic concerns than the policies promoted by democratic socialists.

“We’ve just got to make a better case, long term, about why the things that socialists promise don’t work, and make a better case for that,” Walker said.

Walker said each day-long event will include keynote speakers from various voices in the conservative movement with time dedicated to a question-and-answer session, as well as breakout sessions for students to engage with the ideas presented at the event.

“We’re not there just to inspire or even educate. We’re there to equip,” Walker said. “A key part of our training is how do you take what you’ve heard, take what you’ve learned, and then take it back to your campus, back to your school, back to your community, back online, and actually find ways to bring speakers in, to do activism projects, to persuade people in the classroom, on campus or online, so that you have a multiplier effect.”

Walker said economist Daniel Di Martino, who grew up in socialist Venezuela before he and his family escaped to the United States, will be a recurring speaker at the events and will draw on his own experience to make the case for free markets.

“He’ll be a key part of that just because he’s got such a powerful message,” Walker said.

Walker said reaching students who are still forming their political views requires listening to their concerns and responding directly to people who disagree.

“One of the most effective tools in reaching curious or undecided people is how you respond to people who disagree with you,” Walker said, noting this tactic was something Charlie Kirk did well. “If you let people disagree with you, get up and call you nasty things and then ask a question, and then you calmly but boldly, counter that with the truth…that’s very effective with people who are up in the air because they’re like, ‘Oh, he wasn’t bothered by that, he actually answered that. He countered what I heard before.’”

With the midterms recently finished, Walker said it’s time to prepare for future elections and help young voters be informed about the dangers of socialism.

“We can’t just wait until two years from now, we’ve got to do it now,” Walker said. “And that’s the heart of this Freedom Not Socialism.”

news.title: Joe Biden addresses critics who said he hid his stage 4 cancer diagnosis in upcoming memoir
news.text: Former President Joe Biden responded to accusations that he concealed his cancer diagnosis during his presidency in his new book, according to parts of an excerpt published Tuesday. The former president was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that had spread to his bones in May 2025. "What did surprise me was the cynical twist the story took in the political press and among political commentators," Biden wrote in his upcoming memoir, according to MS NOW. "Almost immediately, the reaction was: ‘You hid it from us.’ ‘You must have known it.’ ‘You’re lying.’ Let me tell you something: There isn’t anyone in this world with stage 4 cancer who doesn’t wish it had been caught sooner." JIMMY FALLON SWIPES AT BIDEN’S UPCOMING MEMOIR, JOKES KAMALA HARRIS WROTE THE END OF IT The memoir, titled "Promise Me, America," is set to be released on Nov. 17. Biden reflects on his four years in the White House in the book, covering the COVID-19 pandemic, the aftermath of the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot, domestic legislation, global diplomacy and his decision to run for re-election before later stepping aside in 2024. The memoir also details the personal deliberations behind his decision to end his 2024 re-election bid. "For anyone to think I would try to ignore or hide a cancer ravaging my body is absurd," Biden wrote, according to the excerpt. "Here are the simple facts. Standard medical protocol is to stop testing men for prostate cancer after the age of seventy." Biden said Sunday that he would not be able to participate in as many conversations about his book as he had hoped because of his treatment. "Some days are better than others. It hasn't stopped me," he said. "But sometimes it slows me down. What that means is, unfortunately, I won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped. However, I’m hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves." "In the daily grind of the White House, it could be difficult to step back and take the long view — because so much was happening every minute," Biden wrote in his book, according to the excerpt. "But now, from my lake house, I am able to slow down and savor the results of my Presidency." JILL BIDEN SAYS FORMER PRESIDENT WILL LIVE WITH STAGE 4 CANCER 'FOR THE REST OF HIS LIFE,' HAS SLOWED DOWN Biden's memoir comes after several books about the 2024 election shed light on the Biden administration's decision-making leading up to the election, including former Vice President Kamala Harris' "107 Days," released in 2025. Harris' book focused mostly on her short campaign for the presidency, but also included some insight into her relationship with Biden and his team. Harris wrote that she felt her decision to remain silent about Biden's 2024 re-election bid had been reckless. "'It’s Joe and Jill’s decision.' We all said that, like a mantra, as if we’d all been hypnotized. Was it grace, or was it recklessness? In retrospect, I think it was recklessness," she said. "The stakes were simply too high. This wasn’t a choice that should have been left to an individual’s ego, an individual’s ambition. It should have been more than a personal decision." news.summary: Former President Joe Biden's responded to critics who accused him of hiding his stage 4 prostate cancer diagnosis from the public in his new book, "Promise Me, America."

news.title: Democrats took the House, Senate and a good deal of Republican pride: So who are the real winners and losers?
news.text: Start with the obvious: Democrats won and Republicans lost. The House was always expected to flip. The Senate was meant to be the nail-biter, and Democrats took it anyway, much of it on Republican turf. They won Senate races in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and South Carolina, a map only the most optimistic Democrats could have drawn, while Alaska and Mississippi may yet join them. Some Republicans are shrugging it off: presidents always lose midterms. They usually do. They lose battleground states and the swing suburbs. They do not usually lose their own strongholds.Winner: Hakeem JeffriesTwo years ago, Hakeem Jeffries was a minority leader watching Republicans run the table in Washington. He is now the presumptive Speaker of the House, the most powerful member of Congress, and is expected to take the gavel in January. By Tuesday, the Associated Press had called 254 seats for Democrats to the Republicans' 165, with 16 still undecided. NBC News projects they will finish with 259, which would be the party's biggest majority in more than three decades. A narrow one would have handed a dozen or so left-wing members a veto over his speakership and his agenda, and several incoming Democrats are still withholding their support. He can now afford at least three dozen defections.The same arithmetic works on legislation: he can lose his party's fringe on a bill and still pass it. Jeffries is set to become the first black Speaker in American history, and he inherits the two things this White House fears most from a Democratic House: control of spending and the power to subpoena.Loser: Donald Trump For two months, Donald Trump told voters to “pretend I'm on the ballot.” He took that message to Texas, Iowa and Kansas, states where his party should never have needed the help. Voters did as they were asked. Trump won Texas by 13.6 points in 2024. Democrat James Talarico won it by 12 last week. Kansas swung 21 points towards the Democrats, and South Carolina swung 22.Mississippi, a state Trump won by 23 points, is still too close to call. About 24 hours after his last plea, the president posted that he “wasn't on the ballot, and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”The exit polls disagree. His approval among midterm voters stood at 37%. Many of his voters also appear to have stayed home: Trump voters made up 44% of last week's electorate, well short of the 49.8% of the vote he won in 2024. Trump has blamed weak candidates.The trouble is most of them were his. He endorsed Ken Paxton over a sitting senator, handpicked Darline Graham and backed Michael Whatley. “It wasn't me” is a hard sell when your name is on every endorsement. Winner: Moderate Democrats If Democrats had a strategy, it was to be boring in all the right places. In Kansas, they ran Adam Hamilton, a first-time candidate who leads the largest United Methodist church in the US. In South Carolina, a paediatrician.In North Carolina, a former two-term governor. In Iowa, a state lawmaker and four-time Paralympian who promised to work with Trump on border security. Independents were ready to punish Trump, and boring gave them a safe place to land.Kamala Harris won independents by just three points in 2024. Last week, Democrats won them 58% to 38%, a 20-point margin. Roughly two-thirds of moderates backed Democrats for the House, up from about six in 10 for Harris.Even Talarico, more liberal than most of the other seat-flippers, won Texas with a friendly, centrist pitch, taking about two-thirds of moderates, most independents and roughly one in 10 Republicans.In Mississippi, District Attorney Scott Colom leads Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 2,500 votes, and that race is likely headed for a legal fight. Losers: Ken Paxton and the MAGA picks Trump's own advisers warned him that Ken Paxton carried too much baggage. He endorsed him anyway, calling the scandal-plagued attorney general “a true MAGA Warrior” and helping him push Senator John Cornyn out in the May runoff.In October, Trump said he had no regrets because “Cornyn would have lost.” We will never know. We do know Paxton lost by 12 points in once-red Texas.The pattern repeated across the map. Majorities of voters in Iowa and Ohio said their Republican candidates were “too supportive” of Trump, and most North Carolina voters said the same of Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman. Nationally, 6% of Republicans voted for Democrats.That sounds small until you get to Texas, where about one in 10 crossed over. When your own voters walk across the aisle at that rate, the problem is not the ground game. It is the candidate and the message. Winner: Progressive Democrats The moderates won the map, but the progressive left won the primaries and a fair number of general elections too. Abdul El-Sayed, a Bernie Sanders ally, beat Mike Rogers in Michigan to become the first Muslim elected to the Senate.Peggy Flanagan held Minnesota and Troy Jackson unseated Susan Collins in Maine, both from the party's progressive wing. In 2010, a Tea Party wave swept into Washington, and its heirs went on to form the Freedom Caucus and make life miserable for Republican speakers.The new progressive class could build the same kind of bloc and do the same to Jeffries. Majorities are easier to win than to manage. Loser: The Graham name in South Carolina For 23 years, Graham meant South Carolina's Senate seat. After Lindsey Graham unexpectedly died in July, his sister Darline took over as interim senator and became Trump's handpicked candidate to keep the seat in the family.It did not go to plan. She flubbed a foreign policy question on the debate stage, and about two-thirds of voters said she lacked the right experience.Even some Republicans hesitated. Others split their tickets, backing Republican Alan Wilson for governor but not Graham. Annie Andrews, a paediatrician, became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since Fritz Hollings in 1998.The family name carried a seat for two decades. It could not carry this campaign.Winners: Kyiv and Brussels The Kyiv Independent's headline said it plainly: “Democrats seize control of Congress in blow to Trump, potential boost for Ukraine.” A Democratic Congress holds the purse strings, and a Democratic Senate will be in no mood to wave through a deal that leaves Ukraine short.German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he was optimistic both parties would now engage more with each other to boost backing for Ukraine.Brussels will also note that tariffs proved a liability at the ballot box, with 66% of voters saying they hurt the US economy. Ukraine is one of the few places Trump could throw Democrats a bone, claim a bipartisan win and look like a dealmaker in the process. Whether he prioritises it over Israel and Iran is another matter. Loser: JD Vance JD Vance went into election day as a Republican front-runner for 2028. He comes out of it as vice president during a historic defeat. The morning after, he offered his own verdict: “The reason we lost is the war.”It is a rare thing for a vice president to say about his own president's war in Iran, and Republican primary voters will read it either as courage or as a man reaching for the exit.Some on the right have already chosen the second reading. A Washington Examiner op-ed called him “fundamentally unfit to lead the Republican Party".It did not help that, asked a week before the election by a young Republican how her generation could afford to start a family, Vance opened with a joke about Jon Husted's backside. Husted lost Ohio. The seat he was defending was Vance's old one. Winners: James Talarico and Jon Ossoff Every wave produces its stars, and this one produced two. James Talarico, a 37-year-old state lawmaker, ended a Democratic drought of more than 30 years in Texas statewide races and summed it up in five words: “We just took back Texas.”Jon Ossoff, 39, did the harder thing in a wave year and made Georgia look easy. He beat Mike Collins by 18 points in a state Trump won two years ago, after raising $126 million more than his opponent.Ossoff insists he has “zero interest in running for president.”Washington has heard that before. Both men will spend the next two years fielding questions about 2028, and both will enjoy it more than they let on. Loser: Trump's inner circle Robert Garcia, who will chair the House Oversight Committee, summed up his plans in two words on election night: “Lawyer up.” His first target, he says, is “the Trump Crime Family.”World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto company, tops that list, along with the Emirati royal nicknamed the “Spy Sheikh", who bought a $500 million stake in it.Donald Trump Jr.'s venture firm, 1789 Capital, is next in the queue. Jamie Raskin, set to chair the Judiciary Committee, says Don Jr. “seems to have a clairvoyant sensibility of exactly who is going to get government contracts.”Jared Kushner, Raskin says, “is a corporate executive that we absolutely will need to talk to.” Aides are on the list too.Garcia says Attorney General Todd Blanche could face a subpoena on “day one” and has promised quick action on alleged pay-to-play involving Kristi Noem and Corey Lewandowski. The White House can lean on executive privilege. The family businesses and their backers cannot. Winners: Ad-makers, TV stations and, finally, viewers OpenSecrets projects this will be the most expensive midterm in American history, at $11.9 billion, about a third more than in 2022. Ohio's Senate race topped $500 million on its own, more than $100 for every vote cast.For the ad-makers, consultants and local TV stations of Ohio, Texas and Georgia, Christmas came in October.The real winners, though, are viewers, who can now watch the evening news or a football game without being told someone's opponent wants to destroy America. Enjoy the quiet. The 2028 primaries start sooner than anyone would like. Loser: Americans who want Washington to get something done Voters sent Washington a to-do list last week. Washington is about to lose it. About eight in 10 registered voters told an AP-NORC poll last month that lowering the cost of living should be one of Congress' highest priorities, and roughly seven in 10 said the same of ending the war with Iran.About half said the same about finding common ground between the parties. What they will get is a stand-off.Trump has already told Fox News what happens next: “They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them.” Democrats are well short of the two-thirds needed to override him, and Senate Republicans still have the numbers to filibuster.That leaves the executive order, even though 71% of voters told exit pollsters they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president. Add the investigations, and expect a lot of hearings and very few laws.Three-quarters of voters already disapprove of Congress, according to the NBC News Exit Poll, and two years of gridlock will not change that. Prices, the war, the deficit and immigration will mostly be kicked down the road to 2028, by which point everyone will be campaigning again.
news.summary: Democrats took the House, the Senate and a good deal of Republican pride last Tuesday night. Here is who came out ahead, and whose hangover lingers on this week.

news.title: Trump’s unedited CBS interview exposes much less 'sane' answers
news.text:
President Donald Trump's recent interview with 60 Minutes about the fallout of the midterms was even worse than what actually made it to air, according to a new report from The New Republic, with an unedited version of the segment exposing answers that come off as much less "sane."

Trump's interview on the newly MAGA-friendly CBS already sparked much alarm and mockery as it aired, with the president making several less-than-flattering answers, including that people complaining about his economy should have been invested in the stock market and that he would rather go to Hell than offer his enemies forgiveness. As it turns out, however, the segment was heavily edited, seemingly in an attempt to sane-wash Trump's responses to conservative interviewer Ross Douthat.

An unedited portion of the segment was initially circulated online by Juliet Jeske, founder of Decoding Fox News, featuring portions of the footage not aired on CBS in black-and-white. As The New Republic explained in its report on the footage, an exchange about the Ukraine war seemed to have been edited to excise "false claims or total fabrications."

When Douthat pressed about what the "biggest obstacle to peace" was, in the broadcast version of the interview, Trump said, "It was the hatred between [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskiy and [Russian President Vladimir] Putin."

As Jeske's post exposed, "much more was left on the cutting room floor."

“I believe that we’re very close to making a deal,” Trump said. “And I think it — two things, if I were president, because as you know, well you’re not going to admit it, it was rigged. That’s why I did it a third time. If I was president that war would have never started.”

Elsewhere in the interview, the program appeared to cut responses in which Trump tried "to puff himself up as tough on Russia and soft on Ukraine.

“Look what I did to them as an example. I gave them the anti-tank busters, right?” the president said. “I’ve given them, in fact there’s an old statement, that [Barack] Obama gave them sheets, and I gave them anti-tank busters, okay? That’s what I gave them,” Trump said.

“But now it’s Europe supplying weapons, not us?” Douthat asked.

“No, it’s us. We’re supplying the weapons, Europe is paying for them,” Trump responded. “Here’s the difference: [Joe] Biden gave them $350 billion worth of cash and weapons. I gave them nothing.”

The New Republic report noted that there is a "deep irony" to Trump's interview being edited in this way, considering that he previously sued CBS, alleging that a 60 Minutes interview with his 2024 opponent, Kamala Harris, had been "selectively edited" in a manner that amounted to "election interference." Paramount Global ultimately opted to settle the suit to the tune of $16 million, despite editing in this manner being commonplace for news programs.

news.title: Kalshi Is Cozy With Trump — But It’s Ramping Up Dem Hires and Campaign Spending
news.text:
Since the start of the year, the prediction betting site Kalshi has two hired former officials from Joe Biden’s White House as a policy adviser and a top lobbyist.

The company’s co-founders have also spent nearly $1 million on donations to federal candidates, with more than a third, or $377,000, going to Democrats like Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., according to a new report.

Kalshi’s spending spree shows how much prediction market sites have ratcheted up their presence in Washington as regulators craft rules for the industry. While the sites’ close relationship with the Trump administration has drawn headlines, the report from the progressive group Demand Progress details how the industry’s influence operation crosses party lines.

The push for bipartisan relationships began months ago, but it could pay dividends as Democrats take over both chambers of a Congress, said Ella Fanger, the corporate power policy adviser for Demand Progress. A betting market critic, Fanger predicted that the companies will keep trying to win allies on both sides of the aisle.

“They’ve been hopeful that they can have Democratic champions for their policy agenda,” she said, “and not just have Trump’s cronies sticking out their necks for them.”

The hiring spree of former Biden officials and spending on Democratic candidates come as prediction markets are facing increasing scrutiny over betting on elections and a spate of suspicious trades from Washington about policy moves and even military action. 

On Tuesday, Democrats on Capitol Hill called for Trump to bar White House staffers from using the betting sites and, with Democrats taking Congress, many observers expect investigations into their use in Washington.

In a statement, Kalshi said it was willing to work “across the ideological spectrum.”

“Kalshi has had substantive conversations with policymakers over the past year regarding legislation that protects consumers, keeps minors off our platform, makes insider trading bans standard across the industry, and ensures the CFTC” — the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — “has the resources they need,” said the company’s head of government relations, John Bivona, a former Democratic congressional staffer and Biden White House official.

“We’ve come out in support of legislation introduced by members across the ideological spectrum,” Bivona said, “and we’ve worked with dozens of lawmakers from both parties on these priorities.”

Hiring Republicans — and Dems

Kalshi and its rival Polymarket are the dominant players in the prediction market industry, which has flourished since Donald Trump became president thanks to his administration’s hands-off approach to regulation.

The ties between the prediction betting sites and Trumpworld go all the way to the president’s inner circle, as evidenced by Donald Trump Jr.’s financial stakes at both competitors.

Polymarket has also hired as a lobbyist a Republican former top official at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The federal regulatory body has, under the Trump administration, sued states for trying to regulate sports betting as gambling.

The Demand Progress report covers Trump Jr.’s ties to the industry, but it also shines a light on the role of former Democratic congressional and executive branch staffers.

Kalshi’s hires have tended toward establishment Democrats. Among them are Stephanie Cutter, a political strategist whose work spanned the Obama and Biden administrations as well as Kamala Harris’s campaign for president. Cutter was tapped as a policy adviser for Kalshi in April. Bivona was hired by Kalshi as its head of government relations in January.

Tripled Lobbying Spend

Overall, Kalshi has spent $1.8 million on lobbying in the first half of 2026, compared to $615,000 in all of 2025, according to the Demand Progress report.

Polymarket spent a relatively meager $180,000 during the same period this year, compared to $360,000 last year.

Fanger, whose group is critical of the prediction markets’ attempts to neutralize state sports gambling regulators, said she is worried that a pliant Congress could approve the Trump administration’s favorable regulations.

“The concern is basically just that we could get legislation that would codify the rulemaking that the CFTC has already begun,” she said, referring to the agency’s efforts to formally exercise jurisdiction over sports, political, cultural, and weather betting contracts. “And we think that it’s important for states to be able to regulate this industry as gambling, which is what it is.”

The industry may need all the lobbyists it can get if progressives gain power in the next Congress. Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., who is angling to chair the House Financial Services Committee, said in a letter last week that she wants to “rein in predatory lending and predatory platforms, including prediction markets, so that our constituents keep more of their hard-earned dollars in their pockets.”

Waters is also a longtime foil to the crypto industry. Crypto currency interests alienated Democrats by spending tens of millions of campaign dollars on Republican Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio, who lost his seat to Democrat Sherrod Brown in the midterm election.

While crypto has lavished money on campaign spending through a super PAC, the prediction market industry has opted for a quieter campaign of smaller donations routed through more traditional channels.

32.5 million people hit on Instagram every day. 88.8 88.8 million hit on Twitter/X every single day and 185 million Facebook hits every single day. And they never figured it out.

Collins appeared nervous that Jones was getting a bit too cocky about spilling the beans, “That’s fascinating Van Jones. Well, I hope you don't get in trouble, but thank you.” Jones chuckled in response, “No, I got permission tonight. Now it can be told. Now it can be told.”

Rub it in you arrogant dweeb @VanJones68 https://t.co/77aKzSZeUH— Joe Vazquez (@JV3MRC) November 10, 2026

Sure, “now it can be told” because voters already got played. The left-wing messaging on affordability was always a crock. BREAKING: Odds of a recession this year plummet to nearly 0% — a record low https://t.co/63hNi3L5Uk— Kalshi (@Kalshi) November 8, 2026

In fact a major MRC Business analysis released October 14 revealed that the average all-items inflation rate during the seven months of the Iran War under President Trump’s second year was 3.6 percent, while core inflation without volatile food and energy prices averaged just 2.6 percent during the same period. During the same time period under Biden’s second year and when Democrats controlled both houses of Congress, average all-items inflation was 8.5 percent while core inflation sat at a ridiculous 6.2 percent. 

“Affordability?” Don’t make us laugh. But the ploy worked anyway, as Jones crowed. “Driving the kitchen table affordability message and tying that to Democrats on a positive and Republicans on a negative. The Republicans never figured out what we were doing.” He continued: “And what that meant was, everywhere you go, people were talking about affordability and they were talking about kitchen-table issues.”

Media lefties and their friends in politics love “affordability” about as much as a vegan loves a steak dinner. The utility of the “affordability” issue was its political expediency, and nothing more.

news.title: Mamdani makes behind-the-scenes moves to shape 2028 Democratic presidential race
news.text: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is quietly working towards a new goal: to become a progressive kingmaker in the burgeoning battle for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination. The socialist mayor of the nation's most populous city, who can't run for president himself because he's not a natural-born U.S. citizen, has been meeting behind closed doors with labor leaders to highlight the need for a union-aligned or left-wing candidate to seek the presidency. The mayor's moves come as he's reportedly said he's uncertain whether progressive champion Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, his close political ally, will run for the White House. According to Axios, which was first to report the news, Mamdani is concerned that if Ocasio-Cortez stays out of the 2028 race, it could leave progressives without a standard-bearer to face off against a more centrist presidential frontrunner in the primary battle. WILL TRUMP SIT OUT MAKING A 2028 ENDORSEMENT IN THE RACE TO SUCCEED HIM? Mamdani, who is seen as a major powerbroker for the left wing of the Democratic Party after his historic 2025 mayoral election victory, argues that the progressive movement can't waste its momentum coming out of last week's trouncing of Republicans in the midterm elections, as Democrats won a massive House majority and control of the Senate. A source familiar with Mamdani's 2028 conversations told Axios the mayor "wants the progressive ecosystem to mobilize quickly, strategically and efficiently if a moderate candidate is clearly on the rise," Meanwhile, Ocasio-Cortez is publicly pumping the brakes on speculation she'll launch a presidential campaign or bid for the Senate in New York, even as a newly formed group of activists is urging her run for the White House. VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS "I think the thing that's important here is the last thing that people want to hear from me or any other politician here is about the next election. And what they actually want to hear from us is about what we are going to do with the electoral results they just gave us on Tuesday," Ocasio-Cortez told reporters Monday night, pointing to the midterms. The comments from Ocasio-Cortez, who was re-elected last week to a fifth term representing parts of New York City, came hours after the formal launch of Ready for AOC, a political group working to encourage her to run for president by showing her she has legions of supporters ready to mobilize on her behalf. "A people-powered movement asking Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for President in 2028. No campaign. No money. Just names," is how the group described itself on social media. But Ocasio-Cortez said voters are more concerned about congressional Democrats' immediate legislative agenda rather than speculating about the next election. "I think people are less concerned about the horse race, and they want to know: What are the investigations we're going to be starting? What is the legislation that we're going to be starting?" she said. Veteran Democratic strategist David Plouffe, campaign manager for former President Barack Obama's landmark 2008 White House victory and a senior advisor on then-Vice President Kamala Harris' 2024 bid, said last week, "If AOC runs, she's going to start, 20-25%, probably. The question is, can she add to that? If she doesn't run, then that is wide open. That's where I think someone like Abdul may say, 'Even though I just won, should I look at it?'" SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Plouffe, who was speaking at a forum hosted by Harvard University's Institute of Politics, was referring to Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who made history last week as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. "That's the thing about this race. It's so wide open that there may be some people run who surprise us. I also think there'll be some people who don't run who'll surprise us," Plouffe added. Ocasio-Cortez said in September that she's weighing what to do next, whether it be a White House run or a bid for the seat currently held by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a fellow Democrat and New Yorker. "I know there is a lot of speculation about what I will decide to do in 2028. I get asked about it nearly every interview and event," Ocasio-Cortez wrote in a fundraising email to supporters. The now-37-year-old lawmaker with a massive social media footprint said in a New York Times interview two months ago that her decision, which could happen sometime after the midterm elections, would come down to answering the question, "Where can I do the most good?" Schumer, who turns 76 later this month, has left his 2028 plans open and has not announced whether he’ll run for sixth six-year term in the Senate. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Ocasio-Cortez isn't the only leading figure on the left who is mulling a presidential run. So is Rep. Ro Khanna of California, a top House progressive. Allies of the soon-to-be six-term congressman last week launched a draft committee called "Run Ro" to build support and raise funds for a potential 2028 presidential campaign.
news.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is meeting with labor leaders to rally progressives around a 2028 presidential candidate if AOC stays out.

news.title: Progressive org launches campaign urging AOC to run for president while progressives eye socialist candidate
news.text: A progressive organization urging Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., to run for president in 2028 has kicked off a campaign to collect signatures nationwide in support of the congresswoman's potential run. Ready for AOC, which describes itself as a "people-powered," "grassroots" and "unaffiliated" organization, launched the campaign Monday, urging supporters of the congresswoman to ask her to run for president. "Movements like this work when they're loud and early — long before the candidate says yes. The proof isn't money. It's names. Yours makes the case louder," the campaign's website states. WATCH: AOC LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID: 'MAYBE, MAYBE NOT' The website boasts 804 signatures as of Tuesday morning, though representatives for the project claim to be aiming for 10,000 community leaders to join their mission, according to the New York Times. The group also claims to have 500 political and union leaders across 35 states on board, the outlet reported. "The goal is to build the infrastructure of a grassroots movement in the case that she decides to run, but also to demonstrate to her that, ‘Look, there is a movement behind you ready to power you to victory should you choose to run for president,'" Ravi Sahai, a spokesman for the group, told the New York Times. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI Ocasio-Cortez herself has been coy about a potential run, but hasn't ruled it out. Asked by Fox News Digital in July if she'd consider running, she replied, "I have genuinely not really weighed seriously anything past the midterm elections." However, following a sweeping blue wave in the midterms that saw voters punch ballots for numerous members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and other far-left candidates, the DSA's ranks are emboldened by the results and vocally making the case that America is ready for a far-left president. MEET THE FAR-LEFT SOCIALISTS COMING TO CONGRESS NEXT YEAR "For so long, we have been told that democratic socialists would be a liability," Gustavo Gordillo, the co-chair of New York City's DSA, said while speaking at an Astoria, Queens watch party on election night. "We've been told for so long that if we elect democratic socialists throughout the country that we won't be able to win races in Texas, in Florida. Tonight, we actually elected a democratic socialist in Tampa in a Republican MAGA-held seat," he bragged, according to state outlet City & State New York. The DSA, which will hold a citywide convention in New York on Nov. 14, will hold a vote on whether the organization will formally push for Ocasio-Cortez to run, Gordillo revealed to a crowd at the watch party, City & State reported. FAR-LEFT SURGE: MAMDANI-BACKED CANDIDATES OUST DEM ESTABLISHMENT INCUMBENTS Despite the buzz, however, Ocasio-Cortez has downplayed speculation following the election, telling reporters that Democrats need to focus on governing over running. "The last thing that people want to hear from me or any other politician is about the next election. What they actually want to hear from us is about what we are going to do with the electoral results they just gave us on Tuesday," she told reporters Monday. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, arguably the DSA's biggest success story, recently told NBC that America is "absolutely" ready for a socialist president. "We have heard time and again over the 10 months that I've been in office here in New York City, that what we're doing here can't work elsewhere, that what people are concerned about here isn't what people are concerned about across the country," Mamdani told NBC's Kristen Welker the day after Election Day. "And what we saw last night is that the struggles of Americans in Atlanta, of Americans in Allentown, are not all that different than the struggles of Americans in Astoria." AOC OPENS UP ABOUT RACE, GENDER IN WEIGHING POSSIBLE 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID Mamdani, who was frequently joined by Ocasio-Cortez while campaigning for mayor in 2025, has not specifically mentioned any potential 2028 candidate by name, but is reportedly meeting with labor and union leaders to organize a potential progressive bloc for 2028. news.title: Rep. Darren Soto survives Republican-drawn map in Florida
news.text:
Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor. 

Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law. 

House Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map. 

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida. 

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The new map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points. 

“Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida showed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement. 

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”

While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party has so far held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. One South Florida contest remains uncalled. The race between GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar and Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez in the Miami-area 27th District had advanced to a recount, with Salazar ahead by less than half a percentage point.

news.title: The Advice Scott Colom Ignored When He Invited Kamala Harris to Mississippi
news.text:
For some of U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom’s advisers, former Vice President Kamala Harris was a political liability. Colom heard the warnings but brought the former vice president to Mississippi anyway along the campaign trial, according to new reports. The decision was a striking show of confidence in a historic political figure whose legacy, influence and place in the Democratic Party remain subjects of debate. It also reopened a larger conversation about race, representation and a party still determining how to move forward.

Harris’s appearance at Columbus High School on Oct. 22 carried significance beyond the campaign. As the first woman, first Black American and first Asian American to serve as vice president, she represents a barrier-breaking chapter in American political history. Her 2024 presidential defeat did not erase that achievement or diminish the questions her candidacy raised about race, gender and access to political power.

For Colom, the decision was also personal. Explaining why he brought Harris to Columbus rather than a larger metropolitan area, he had a simple response for the Mississippi Free Press: “You know what I told them? ‘Why not?’” His hometown, he explained, helped shape the values he carries into public life.

Harris made the purpose of her visit equally clear. “Mississippi matters,” she told the crowd, connecting Colom’s campaign to concerns about healthcare, rising costs and political accountability. She urged voters to turn frustration into participation, declaring, “We have the ability to do something.”

RELATED: Exclusive: Kamala Harris Is Teaming Up With the NAACP to Get Voters Ready for November

Two Democrat sources familiar with Colom’s campaign told the Mississippi Free Press that his advisers did not want Harris involved. Still, the visit brought practical benefits. 

Colom told CNN that Harris’s appearance helped attract attention to Mississippi’s struggling rural hospitals. “Now, if I did a press conference outside one of those projects and called her out for voting against the money, but showing at the press conference bragging about the projects, no reporter would come,” Scott said. “And the reason I noticed [is] because I tried that, and nobody came.”

Still, the episode raises a larger question for Democrats. Harris remains a historic figure, but her political future is unsettled. As the party looks toward its next chapter, it must reckon with the lessons of her candidacy and the voters who felt represented by her historic rise.

Democrats still have work to do: rebuilding trust, investing in communities beyond traditional battlegrounds and addressing the barriers that continue to shape political representation. Colom’s decision offers a reminder that writing off a political figure–or an entire state– has consequences. 

As of now, he leads Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Senate race by just over 2,600 votes. Officials have not called the race yet.

Despite advisers’ concerns, Mississippi’s Scott Colom brought Kamala Harris to Columbus, raising questions about political strategy, representation and the party’s future.

news.title: 'This is how you rig elections’: Stephen Miller’s wife slams Wikipedia for scrubbing Abdul El-Sayed's past
news.text:
Political campaigns spend tens of millions trying to clean up their candidates' public image. Campaign managers buy TV ads. They test slogans in focus groups and flood mailboxes with leaflets that portray swamp creatures as borderline saints. But in modern elections, those traditional PR blitzes matter far less than what happens on a single online reference page.

The recent election of Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan offers a textbook case study in how public memory gets manipulated right before voters step into the booth. In recent months, a rather prolific Wikipedia editor using the handle CopyleftEverything has carried out a massive makeover of El-Sayed's profile page. Between October 10 and November 1, the spin merchant made 17 edits to the page, adding over 15,000 bytes of content while the entry racked up roughly 1.64 million views. 

Wikipedia restricted edits to El-Sayed’s entry to protected user classes.

The edits weren't routine formatting touch-ups or fixing minor typographical errors. 

The account removed a 1,642-byte section describing El-Sayed’s attempt to hire Lenore Goldman as a Jewish community liaison, alongside documented tension between his team and Michigan's Jewish community. It sanitized the description of El-Sayed's ally Hasan Piker, a political commentator who has repeatedly claimed that America deserved 9/11, from a controversial left-wing streamer to a neutral commentator. It inserted favorable notes regarding endorsements from former president and current podcaster Barack Obama as well as Kamala Harris, who remains the nation's most reliable provider of unintentional comedy. 

CopyleftEverything also altered the wording surrounding El-Sayed's medical credentials, shifting the text from stating he had never held a medical license to stating he simply hadn't pursued one.

Replying on X to reporting about the extensive edits by narrative manipulation analyst Ashley Rindsberg, Katie Miller, wife of new White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, responded bluntly: "This is how you rig elections."

She's right.

A difference large enough to drive a fleet of ambulances through exists between never obtaining a medical license and choosing not to pursue one. The first states an objective administrative fact; the second offers an incredibly accommodating narrative.

When a candidate’s past includes plenty of controversy, voters rely on search engines and encyclopedia entries for the facts. Removing documented history regarding relations with local faith communities or altering official background details converts a reference tool into a shadow campaign platform. 

Public records show El-Sayed’s father, Mohamed El-Sayed, served as a board member for the Islamic charity Life for Relief and Development. In 2014, the charity reached a $780,000 federal settlement over unauthorized financial transfers to Iraq during 2002 to 2003. Investigative reports entered into evidence during the 2008 Holy Land Foundation trial linked early leadership within that organization to Muslim Brotherhood networks in North America. Furthermore, his father-in-law, Tayeb Jukaku, served on the board of the Council on American-Islamic Relations in Michigan. Given El-Sayed's recent election victory and his cozy relationship with the dangerous organization, Americans in Michigan and beyond are entitled to ask questions and expect honest answers. When digital entries are deliberately distorted right before an election, voters lose the ability to assess that record for themselves. 

RELATED: Don't trust the socialists — tech won the midterms

 Tom Baker/Getty Images 

Interestingly but not surprisingly, Wikipedia restricted edits to El-Sayed’s entry to protected user classes, while Mike Rogers’ page, his Republican opponent’s, remained open to edits. On November 1, the same active account inserted material directly into Rogers’ entry about allegations of campaign funding. 

The future of fudging

The platform’s left-leaning favoritism becomes critical when evaluating the future of AI. 

Modern AI models sometimes invent facts out of thin air, but that's becoming rarer by the day. They train heavily on open-source web repositories like Wikipedia, and sites like Wikipedia know it well. "In the AI era, Wikipedia has never been more valuable," the Wikimedia Foundation proudly proclaims. When a candidate's background gets scrubbed from the source site, AI tools mistake the glorified propaganda for baseline truth.

When voters ask ChatGPT or Claude about a candidate’s record, the algorithm regurgitates the edited version without mentioning the deleted paragraphs. Digital reputation management no longer requires buying commercial ads. One only needs to maintain control over a few key web entries just before the polls open. 

To those who dismiss these editing skirmishes as nothing more than a nothingburger, the real danger isn't just that a single web page was modified but that the public history of an incoming U.S. senator was actively altered without disclosure, leaving voters with an incomplete record on Election Day. Anyone who consulted Wikipedia before voting for El-Sayed has every reason to feel cheated. 

When reference platforms claim impartiality while serving as pre-election PR vehicles, the entire foundation of an informed electorate crumbles. Conservatives have long argued that media institutions operate in a hostile, contemptible manner. Their arguments are grounded in reality. 

If an anonymous editor can alter medical credentials, remove documented community clashes, and insert campaign talking points without oversight, political campaigns will stop spending money on traditional ads altogether. An editor will simply hire digital squads to rewrite candidate histories in real time, ensuring that voters only ever see what the campaign wants them to see. 

Democratic accountability relies entirely on voters having access to facts, no matter how ugly they may be, before making their choice at the ballot box. When those facts are systematically tampered with on the world's primary reference source, voters lose their ability to hold candidates accountable for their past sins. 

Those who control the past control the future. And in the digital information age, the left appears to hold the upper hand.
