news.title: Latino 'anger,' 'peer pressure' helped Democrats win, group says
news.text:
Widespread economic worry, including a sense that President Donald Trump had failed to deliver on affordability, helped fuel a broad shift of Latino votes to Democrats in Arizona and elsewhere, a national Hispanic advocacy organization found.

About 16% of Latinos who backed Trump in 2024 switched and voted for Democratic congressional candidates, while only 1% of Latinos who supported Vice President Kamala Harris changed to Republicans, polling for UnidosUS found.

It was a similar dynamic in Arizona’s governor’s race, with Latinos moving more toward the Democrat, Gov. Katie Hobbs, than Republican Andy Biggs, by a 20% to 2% margin.

“Anger about the state of the economy and immigration actions drove Hispanics to the polls, not party loyalty or ideology,” said Clarissa Martinez, a vice president for the group’s Latino vote initiative. “That anger led to unprecedented Democratic wins.”

The findings from UnidosUS join other efforts to understand the historic, nationwide electoral rout for Republicans, including in Arizona.

The New York Times, for example, noted a “monumental” surge in voters under 30. The left-leaning Brookings Institution suggested that a significant slice of disaffected Republican voters “stayed home, opening the door for highly motivated Democrats to score massive gains.”

In its survey of Latino voters, UnidosUS saw economic issues occupying the top five issues on voters’ minds. Add to it lopsided opposition to the war in Iran and immigration enforcement actions — and a favorable view of Democrats.

Trump’s 2024 win was partially due to a surprisingly strong showing with Latino voters, especially men. That demographic swung more heavily to the left this time.

The survey pointed to an electorate that helped bring heavy losses to Republicans up and down the ballot in Arizona. The group surveyed 337 Latino voters in Arizona. It conducted similar surveys in California, Florida, Michigan and Texas.

Democrats won statewide offices, even down to the mine inspector. They flipped both chambers of the Arizona Legislature for the first time in 60 years and two Republican-held seats in Congress to give the state delegation a Democratic majority.

“One of the big takeaways … was the higher turnout of Latino men for Democrats compared to women,” said Enrique Davis Mazlum, the state director for UnidosUS in Arizona.

Family conversations helped bring about the shift, he said.

“I think there was a collective peer pressure of families toward those who voted for Republicans two years ago. They also saw their friends, family members, some of them being detained, losing work, et cetera. … I think they internalized it and they took it to the polls.”

According to the UnidosUS poll, 73% of Latinos voted for Democrats in congressional races. Hobbs got 70% of their votes.

About half of their respondents reported economic difficulty making ends meet or worse. Trump only had the approval of 26%, while 72% disapproved of his performance in the White House. The numbers were little better for Republicans in Congress.

At the same time, 70% of Latino men — even more than Latino women — felt the Democratic Party cares “a great deal” about the Latino community.

news.title: Indian-Americans didn't come home to Democrats; they just walked away from Trump
news.text:
Last week’s midterms seem to mark a Democratic triumph. With seven Senate seats flipped, including Texas and the Carolinas, a blue majority in the House and Senate evoke jubilation reminiscent of 2008’s Obama-era millennial optimism.
Particularly with Indian-American voters, headlines that once framed the community as “natural conservatives” and “ditching Democrats” now proclaim a “swing back” and a “progressive turn” following last week’s election results.
The sentiment is clear; for nearly a decade, it seems that the Indian-American vote has been on a steady trajectory to the right until this midterm’s Democratic sweep.
It’s easy to see where the narrative holds up. Trump’s administration ironically has some of the highest visibility of Indian-American politicians, anchored by a once very public cordial friendship between Trump and Modi.
Prominent figures like Second Lady Usha Vance, FBI Director Kash Patel, and Jay Bhattacharya, Director of the National Institutes of Health, help run a government fuelled by anti-immigration sentiment and exclusionary politics. The story writes itself.
However, with over 62 per cent of the diaspora intending to vote blue, the optics on last week’s midterms symbolised an apparent liberal reversal for Indian-Americans. While there was a shift in Indian-American voting patterns, the midterms sweep isn’t the Democratic homecoming many think it is.
Despite the optics, Indian-Americans have historically always skewed Blue with a clear majority of 60 per cent voting Democrat in every Presidential election since 2012. The red herring in the “Indian-Americans are turning conservative” story lies in its male voters.
The prodigal son returns 
In 2024, four in ten Indian-American males voted for Trump. The sentiment seemed rooted in being the model minority; wealthy, educated and legal, unlike the ones being targeted.
Two years into his second presidency term, with a freeze on H-1B petitions (Indians receive about 71 per cent of visa approvals) at Texas state institutions and a $100,000 fee on new petitions, the rhetoric faltered.
Since then, Carnegie/YouGov's survey finds that Republican support in Indian-American males under 40 dropped from 40 per cent to 23 per cent in 2024 and halved from 32 per cent to 16 per cent in men over 40 in the past 9 months. While the shift is significant, it is disillusionment rather than devotion driving the change.
19 per cent of Indian-American men regret voting for Trump in 2024, with more than a third of Indian-Americans leaning Democrat being primarily moved by antipathy for the Republican Party.
With disapproval ratings among the community at 71 per cent in January, Trump’s claim that Republicans would have “won in a landslide” had his name been on the ballot may be a counterfactual he is not willing to test.
The flip? Gender not party 
The real reversal is not one of blue and red, but rather a question of gender. In 2024, Kamala Harris’ margin amongst Indian-American women was 31 points higher than men.
By October 2026, younger women’s support was 10 percentage points down at 58 per cent compared to January while younger men’s Democratic support increased by 4 percentage points to 64 per cent.
Even among older voters, Democratic support only increased by 8 percentage points to 58 per cent in women over 40, compared to a 15 percentage point increase to 68 per cent in men over 40 between January and October 2026.
Indian-American women cooled in contrast to other American women. However, compared to 2024, there is a significantly weakened attachment to the party amongst women.
Democratic identification has slipped from 50 per cent to 46 per cent. Now Indian-American men are just as likely, if not more likely than women to vote blue.
Interestingly the gender gap has flipped amongst Indian-American voters, with men of both age groups surpassing women in Democratic support as of October 2026, deterring the liberal return rhetoric even further.
This staunch difference from 2024 begs the question; why was it that with a South Asian woman on the Democratic presidential ballot in 2024 Indian-American men hesitated to vote, but not in 2026?
Ideas over identity
Kamala Harris did worse in the community as a presidential nominee than her counterpart with only 61 per cent support as opposed to 72 per cent for Joe Biden.
Less than a tenth of her Indian-American supporters cited her heritage as motivation. Identity doesn’t seem to be a core tenet resonating with the Indian-American vote, despite the visible spotlight on South Asian politicians on both sides of the race.
Mamdani’s mayoral win came largely from his politics with only 15 per cent of Indian-Americans viewing him primarily as a candidate of Indian-origin.
Several politicians won big in the midterms from Pramila Jayapal’s re-election to Nithya Raman’s projected L.A mayoral win. It seems that ideas take precedence over identity politics amongst Indian-American voters.
Conversely, while identity alone may not win the community’s vote, threats to Indian-American identity have pushed voters away from the right. Vivek Ramaswamy, who lost the Ohio governor race as a Republican, received verbal attacks on his identity from within his party.
Texas Railroad Commission candidate Bo French referred to South Asians celebrating a college football victory as “a problem far worse than anyone imagined” on X. The turn to Blue is an aversion rather than a reversal.
The optics seem to have misread Indian-American voters not once but twice. In 2024, with the discourse that the community swayed heavily conservative, and again in 2026, suggesting a strong recourse to the Democratic Party.
There seems to be more of a discrepancy between men and women within the diaspora rather than shifting party alignment.
Democratic support in the community is not a vote of blind faith, but rather a vote against the current administration.
It remains to be seen whether disillusionment alone can carry the Indian American vote to 2028.
(The author is a writer, journalist, and independent media creator. Views expressed are personal and do not necessarily reflect those of Firstpost.)

news.title: Why did California's billionaire tax fail to surf the blue wave?
news.text:
Late Monday, The Associated Press determined that California voters had rejected Prop 40, the proposed billionaire wealth tax I wrote about last week. Given the big blue wave we saw during the midterms, why did this tax on billionaires fail to surf to victory?

To make sense of the results, I went back to the two economists I spoke with last week: UC Berkeley's Gabriel Zucman, a leading champion of wealth taxes, and Stanford's Joshua Rauh, a prominent critic of Prop 40.

Last week, they disagreed on what this wealth tax on billionaires would do to California's economy and tax revenue. Now comes the sequel, in which they disagree on what the results say about the politics of wealth taxes.

Their debate could foreshadow a bigger one in the next Democratic presidential primary: should the party embrace a wealth tax?

Did billionaire money tip the scales?

Zucman blames the corrosive influence of money for Prop 40's failure.

"I am not surprised," Zucman says. Opponents of Prop 40 spent almost $400 million fighting it, including spending on competing ballot measures, making it one of the most expensive ballot initiative fights in history.

"The money spent by the billionaires was critical," Zucman says. "Anyone who lives in California has been carpet-bombed by a deluge of ads. One can easily see how this could be pivotal in such a closely contested ballot."

But didn't Democrats win plenty of races this cycle despite huge sums spent against them? In Texas, for example, Elon Musk alone poured more than $150 million into defeating Democrat James Talarico. And Talarico ended up winning his Senate race by a comfortable margin. Why would money have been so decisive with Prop 40 and not in other races around the nation?

For one, Zucman says, the spending gap was much bigger in the fight over Prop 40. "The billionaires spent more than $300 million on ads versus negligible sums on the other side," Zucman says. "On TV and in their mailboxes, voters were exposed only to the anti-tax arguments. This was very different from the other midterm races: in those races, when spending was high (e.g., Talarico vs. Paxton in Texas) it was high on both sides, even if unevenly. The net difference in spending was considerably larger for Prop 40."

It's also possible that money can matter more in ballot initiatives than in races between candidates. Analysts have complained for decades that California's ballot initiative system is too easily manipulated by special interest groups. The nitty-gritty details of specific policies can get complicated, and many voters don't take the time to get educated on them. That can give well-funded advertising campaigns more power to shape their views.

In candidate races, meanwhile, voters can at least fall back on name recognition or party labels, which give them an easy mental shortcut — what social scientists call a "heuristic" — when making decisions at the ballot box. Even when they know little about the candidates, they usually know which party they prefer.

But Prop 40 didn't come with the same clear partisan signal. In fact, prominent Democrats, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, came out against it. Newsom said he favored a national minimum tax on billionaires instead.

Or was this tax policy itself the problem?

"Popular opinion on wealth taxes is clearly not as strong as proponents thought," Rauh says.

Rauh questions whether money and advertising can really explain Prop 40's poor showing. He compared support for the tax with support for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. In some of "the most progressive Bay Area counties," he says, Harris won overwhelming support while Prop 40 won much less. This gap between support for Harris and support for Prop 40 was bigger there than it was in other Democratic-leaning counties across the state.

If advertising was the main explanation for this tax's poor showing, he argues, why was the gap so much bigger in the Bay Area? Sure, he says, advertisers may have done more targeting there, but he thinks the uneven pattern across the state casts doubt on the idea that advertising was the decisive factor.

"[T]he counties with the largest defections are actually the ones whose residents are most likely to know a billionaire, to work for one, or to have watched one move to Texas or Florida," Rauh writes in a recent post. "The simple reading is that proximity to the people being taxed, and to the businesses they fund, made voters more skeptical of the tax relative to their baseline politics."

For Rauh, that skepticism points to a broader conclusion: "The electorate even in progressive California has shown that it isn't ready for a wealth tax," he says.

More moderate Democratic voters, especially in affluent areas like the Bay Area, may simply dislike this novel way of taxing rich people in America and the consequences it could have. After all, this policy idea has divided Democrats before. During the 2020 presidential primary, Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders both championed wealth taxes, but rivals like Sen. Cory Booker and Michael Bloomberg opposed them. Joe Biden said he didn't oppose a wealth tax on the campaign trail, but early in his presidency, he declined to pursue Sen. Warren's wealth tax proposal.

Or maybe voters weren't rejecting the idea of a wealth tax per se. Maybe they were rejecting the particulars of this wealth tax.

For one thing, Prop 40 was a one-time tax, and it earmarked its projected revenue in ways that drew opposition from traditional Democratic allies. It allocated 90% of the revenue to health care, leaving only 10% for food assistance and education-related programs.

That helped put some typically left-leaning organizations in the opposition camp. For example, the California Teachers Association, a powerful teachers union. It argued that Prop 40 shortchanged public schools and did "not provide the sustainable and long-lasting funding that our schools and communities deserve."

Meanwhile, Prop 40 would have taxed billionaires at the state level. Supporters of a national approach argue that a wealth tax would be more effective at the national level because it's harder to leave America than it is to move to another state.

When Newsom came out against Prop 40 back in June, he wrote, "Wealth is movable, and it shops for the state with the lowest taxes. The fight belongs at the federal level, where this broken system was created in the first place."

Where does the wealth tax movement go from here?

Despite Prop 40's defeat, Zucman believes the wealth tax movement is far from over.

"With the blue wave nationally, the billionaire tax is going to be front and center in the new Congress," Zucman says. "Many of the newly elected Democratic senators have been campaigning on curbing the power and influence of billionaires. One can reasonably expect to see significant progress in the next two years."

Rauh also expects to see more wealth tax proposals in the coming Congress. But with President Trump in the White House, he sees little chance of one becoming law anytime soon.

"It will be the 2028 election that will really demonstrate the extent to which the public wants wealth taxation, as those proposals will likely feature prominently in political debate," Rauh says.

But even if wealth tax supporters win over voters, Rauh stresses they would encounter another big hurdle: the courts. He argues a federal wealth tax would constitute "a direct tax," a kind of tax that is subject to crippling constitutional restrictions.

As I explained in this 2019 Planet Money newsletter, the U.S. Constitution requires that "direct taxes" go through a complicated rigamarole in order to be constitutional. Specifically, the share of a direct tax's total revenue collected from each state has to match its share of the national population. That could mean wildly different tax rates depending on where people live.

This weird rule's history is tangled up with slavery. In one early Supreme Court case, one justice described it as basically a concession to Southern states seeking to limit federal taxation of their land and enslaved people.

The 16th Amendment exempted income taxes from this requirement. But that amendment doesn't mention wealth taxes.

Legal scholars disagree over whether this rule would doom a federal wealth tax. Is a wealth tax even a "direct tax"? That early Supreme Court case involved a tax on horse-drawn carriages that George Washington signed into law in 1794. The Court upheld it, a precedent wealth tax supporters point to today. For more on that story, listen to the Planet Money episode I did, "The Carriage Tax."

Stay tuned for more wealth tax coverage in the Planet Money newsletter in the future. We guess this movement isn't going away.

news.title: El-Sayed's election victory was can't-miss history for this Detroiter
news.text:
When retired Wayne County Judge Craig Strong says he is a “student of history,” the lifelong Detroiter is talking about history that he has absorbed, which goes well beyond the pages of history books. 

For example, on June 23, 1963, a 15-year-old Strong and his parents, the late Erman and Manila Geraldine Powers Strong, were among the 125,000 people that attended the Detroit March To Freedom that ended downtown at Cobo Hall, where Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered a version of his “I Have A Dream” speech for the first time. 

Fast-forward to April 1994 and Strong could be found in South Africa serving as an observer for the United Nations during the election that would ultimately lead to Nelson Mandela being inaugurated as the country’s first Black president on May 10, 1994, after Mandela had spent 27 years in South African prisons during his fight against apartheid. 

And on the evening of Tuesday, November 3 — and into the early morning of Wednesday, Nov. 4 — Strong was on the scene for another major political event during an election night party held by Michigan Democrats at The Department at Hudson’s in downtown Detroit.

The long hours of sitting in one spot, mixed with moments when the 79-year-old Strong was required to abruptly rise to his feet, tested a body which has endured back surgery. 

But Strong says the physical discomfort was all worth it when the history he came to witness was secured with the election of the former Wayne County and Detroit health director Abdul El-Sayed, a child of Egyptian immigrants, who became the first Muslim ever elected to the U.S. Senate after defeating Republican Mike Rogers. The victory came after a highly contentious campaign where El-Sayed faced accusations of antisemitism and was the target of Islamophobic attacks.

“I had to witness history,” stated Strong, who also had attended a rally for El-Sayed a day earlier at the Majestic Theater in Midtown Detroit. “America is finally becoming a real melting pot. And the principle that ‘All men are created equal’ is coming around and is on display at this important moment in our history.” 

To fully understand Strong’s feelings about the principles of justice, equality and diversity requires some knowledge of Strong’s personal history. The stylish gentleman, raised and nurtured on Detroit’s Old West Side, who at the time of his retirement was Wayne County’s longest-tenured judge (1978-2020), also is the grandson of a woman who was born into America’s institution of slavery. 

“I’m the grandson of a slave; my father’s mother was born into slavery. My father was the last of her 12 children, and then my parents would have their first four children, and almost 10 years later, I’m born, so there’s that big gap," Strong explained in a June 4, 2002 Detroit Free Press story. "At my swearing-in, my mother said she wished my grandmother could see this because here’s a woman who had no rights with a grandson who is protecting people’s rights. I teared up on that one.” 

Strong says he thinks of his grandmother often. However, as he spoke during the afternoon of November 4, there were no tears, but instead an undeniable enthusiasm could be heard in his voice as Strong went into further detail about what he witnessed while “showing up” for El-Sayed on election night.

“I saw a racial mixture, and a gender mixture, and I saw a broad age range represented, including many young people, which is so important,” said Strong, who did not leave the festivities until 2 a.m. “The senator-elect represents all of us, so it was important for him to see us because believing is seeing. And we have to be able to help him help us.” 

More from Scott Talley: Abdul El-Sayed was making history and Craig Strong had to 'show up'

Nov. 3 has been an historic election day for Michigan and Detroit

Photos taken with El-Sayed are now a part of Strong's cherished collection

When asked to describe his future plans to support the work of El-Sayed, who ran on a progressive platform centered on universal healthcare, corporate accountability and reshaping American foreign policy, Strong said: “I haven’t thought that through yet, but I plan to get in where I can fit in to help our community.”

Nonetheless, Strong already took one important action that has been a consistent part of his lifelong journey through history, when he added photos that he took with El-Sayed at the rally and election celebration to his robust celebrity photo collection that spans many decades. 

The collection includes photos that Strong has taken with some of the most famous people to ever walk the earth, including Muhammad Ali, Barack Obama, Rosa Parks, Bill Clinton, Oprah Winfrey, Archbishop Desmond Tutu, Jesse Jackson, Dick Gregory, Mike Tyson, James Brown, Magic Johnson, Kamala Harris and George H.W. Bush, just to name a few.

These images tell the stories that Strong's grandmother never could have imagined. But Strong says the collection also reflects his commitment to another sacred principle that connects him to his family and the Detroit West Side community that poured into him. 

“People always ask me how I was able to take so many pictures with famous people, and I tell them I have met those people through service and service to my community,” said Strong, whose personal record of service includes being a retired commander in the U.S. Navy Reserve, where he presided over court-martial proceedings as a military judge. “I tell young people all the time that in order to grow, you have to show up and be a part of life, and that starts with service.” 

Scott Talley is a native Detroiter, a proud product of Detroit Public Schools and a lifelong lover of Detroit culture in its diverse forms. In his second tour with the Free Press, which he grew up reading as a child, he is excited and humbled to cover the city’s neighborhoods and the many interesting people who define its various communities. Contact him at stalley@freepress.com. Read more of Scott's stories at www.freep.com/mosaic/detroit-is/. Please help us grow great community-focused journalism by becoming a subscriber.

news.title: Developing! The Democrats Are (Almost) the Working-Class Party Again
news.text:
Some commentators see this glass as half-empty. “The Democratic Coalition Still Has a Class Problem,” wrote Jared Abbott of the Center for Working Class Politics in Jacobin. Ruy Teixeira, co-author with John Judis of the 2023 book Where Have All the Democrats Gone?, bemoaned in The Free Press the likelihood that Democrats will move recklessly to the left (and therefore away from “winnable voters,” by whom he means working class voters). Indeed, a few days before the election Teixeira predicted in The Washington Post that a blue wave “may cripple” the Democrats because “the better they do in 2026, the more likely they are to ignore their party’s weaknesses with working-class and rural voters.” For Teixeira, who’s been drifting rightward in recent years, this borders on self-caricature.

The exit polls show a substantial improvement for Democrats drawing working class voters compared to 2024. In 2024, 43 percent of the non-college vote went to Kamala Harris and to House Democrats, against 56 percent for Trump and House Republicans. That means the Democrats narrowed the Republican advantage from 13 points to two points. In the 2022 midterms, the Republican advantage was a similar 12 points (43 percent for Democrats and 55 percent for Republicans). In essence, Democrats have returned to the status quo of 2020, when Joe Biden, a candidate with strong blue-collar credentials, captured 48 percent of non-college voters to Trump’s 50 percent. (If you go by the voter database Catalyst’s figures for 2024, which are better than exit polls, the Republican advantage that year was more like 11 points. But you get the idea.)

I have written previously that over the past century no Democrat, excepting Biden in 2020, ever won the presidency without winning a majority of non-college voters—and that Biden won under the non-replicable circumstance of Trump’s bungling the deadly Covid pandemic. Judged in that light, the Democrats’ 48 percent support among working-class voters is indeed disappointing, because 48 percent won’t likely be sufficient to elect a Democrat president in 2028. If, in a blowout midterm victory, Democrats failed to secure the working-class majority that’s probably necessary to win the presidency, what hope is there next time?

news.title: Leftists Weren’t the Only Ones Who Moderated In the Midterms
news.text:
This all feels a bit silly. For starters, Democrats won enough for everyone to have something to celebrate. Democratic Socialists won well beyond New York City’s so-called “Commie corridor.” DSA has sent six new representatives to the House, and elected its members as mayors in Washington D.C. and Los Angeles. But most candidates who won were not DSA members or endorsed by DSA chapters. Many took up positions that progressives generally oppose while also bashing billionaires and Big Tech. The vast majority of voters, moreover, were not voting for one faction or another because most people don’t possess coherent political ideologies. These intra-party debates matter mostly insofar as they shape how Democrats will use their Congressional majority, and—relatedly—whether they can convince voters to keep voting for Democrats in 2028. As moderate centrists make the case that moderate centrists won, they’re accordingly arguing that Democrats should govern as moderate centrists. 

Vibes-based assessments of who counts as a moderate, however, and what it means “to moderate”—feel relatively divorced from the material factors that determine how politicians campaign and govern once they win. Although much of the discourse around Tuesday’s results has focused on how candidates “moderated” certain traditionally left-wing positions in order to win, there’s a case to be made that centrists walking back their own unpopular stances made just as big of a difference.

On one critical issue—U.S. support for Israel—Democrats have moderated enormously over the last two years. The party wouldn’t even agree to let a Palestinian State Representative from Georgia address the Democratic National Convention in 2024. Democrats’ own autopsy of their loss that year concluded that Kamala Harris’s support for the Biden administration’s continued funding of Israel’s genocide in Gaza cost her critical support, particularly among younger voters. Public opinion has changed rapidly since then. An October 2024 Gallup poll of Americans’ views on the Middle East found that 51 percent sympathized more with Israelis, compared to the 27 percent that sympathized more with Palestinians. When Gallup polled the same question this year, 41 percent sympathized more with Palestinians, while 36 percent sympathized more with Israelis.

news.title: Arellano: Raman's victory was a resounding rebuke to L.A.'s Latino political establishment
news.text: When Angelenos chose Nithya Raman as their next mayor, Karen Bass wasn't the only establishment pillar that was resoundingly rebuked. Here in the country's Latino capital, the metropolis that delivered California its first Latino U.S. senator and pioneered the type of winning political machine that Latinos across the country replicated for decades, almost all the city's Latino power brokers — politicians, nonprofit leaders, union activists, celebrities — bet big on longtime ally Bass, only to now find themselves on the outside looking in. All that might and hype delivered worse than nada for Bass, who finished first in the June primary thanks in part to Latino support, winning 35 Latino-majority neighborhoods compared with just seven for Raman. The reverse happened in last week's general election, with Raman winning many of the city's key Latino neighborhoods — South L.A. to the Eastside, Pico-Union to Wilmington — according to a Times analysis of precinct data. It was a fitting dénouement to Mayor Bass' one term in office, and the capstone of a terrible four-year run for L.A.'s Latino political establishment, beginning with the leak of a profane, racist conversation that disgraced four top politicos. Bass should have run as far away as possible from our caudillos y caudillas. But she just couldn't quit them. Take an Oct. 24 lunchtime rally at Plaza Del Valle in Panorama City, the nexus for the fabled San Fernando Valley Latino political machine. Volunteers handed out “Latinos Con Bass” signs to customers and store owners. An all-star roster of elected officials — City Councilmembers Monica Rodriguez and Imelda Padilla, Assemblymember Celeste Rodriguez (no relation to Monica) and Rep. Luz Rivas — gathered in a community room to make the case that Bass was the best choice. “You have tías and cousins and primos that call you, ‘Who should I vote for? What do I do? How do I fill out the ballot?’” Rivas told a crowd of about 60, most of whom were not Latino. “You need to remind them Mayor Karen Bass is the right leader.” “This is where we win elections,” Rodriguez asserted, describing the mayor — whom she bitterly opposed until fellow Councilmember Raman entered the race — as a “Valley girl” and the election as “our moment.” The enthusiasm level struggled to exceed that of a line at the DMV. Half an hour later and a few miles east in Sylmar, a very different scene was unfolding. DJ Danny Guerrero blasted quinceañera classics like “Vivir mi Vida” and “Come On Let’s Go” by Pacoima native Ritchie Valens as Raman's team hosted a canvasada — free tacos for everyone to fuel an afternoon of canvassing. L.A. Unified school board member Kelly Gonez was the only elected official at the Carpenters Local 818 training center. The others were union members, Latino hipsters or kids too young to vote. “Her passion to protect our community — that compassion resonated with me,” said Guerrero, a 21-year-old Cal State Northridge political science major who helps undocumented college students at his school's Dream Center. “I advocate for that in my life, and I see Nithya doing that. She meets us where we’re at.” Guerrero cheered as Raman kicked off her remarks with an “¡Hola, Sylmar!,” pronouncing the "y" like an "i" the way a Spanish speaker would. The candidate shouted out Latino Valley icons like Lenchita’s, Tia Chucha’s Centro Cultural and even Plaza Del Valle. But she received the biggest cheers when she said, “La communidad latina merece más.” Latinos deserve more. In the end, Raman captured most of the precincts in Padilla's and Rodriguez's districts even after the two council members whacked away at her through the election like brats hogging the piñata stick at a birthday party. Without institutional support, Raman focused on a new generation of Latino leaders who are not part of the traditional political machines. “Maybe they [Latino establishment leaders] felt obligated to back her,” Rocío Rivas said of Bass. The L.A. Unified school board member and democratic socialist endorsed Raman and attended her election night party at the Greek Theatre, where a crowd of hundreds chanted, “Sí se puede." “Or maybe they’re not as connected to the community as they once were," Rivas added. The trouble for the establishment started in 2022 when three City Council members and a powerful union leader became pariahs after starring in the audio leak scandal. That same year, democratic socialist upstarts Hugo Soto-Martínez and Eunisses Hernandez won City Council seats, despite a lack of support from Chicanosauruses who mocked their chances. In January 2024, former City Councilmember Jose Huizar — once a rising star with aspirations for higher office — was sentenced to 13 years in prison after pleading guilty to corruption charges. In the fall of that year, Eastside Assembly and City Council seats held by Latinos for decades went to Filipina Americans Jessica Caloza and Ysabel Jurado. Meanwhile, former Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa's campaign for governor sputtered out with just 1% of the vote. In the race to succeed Nury Martinez, who resigned from the City Council after the audio leak, Padilla won with backing from the Valley Latino political machine. Marco Santana lost to Padilla in the primary. despite an endorsement from Raman, and supported Raman's mayoral campaign. “The mayor ran on a very institutional playbook of getting a bunch of Latino politicians together so they could tell Latinos how to vote,” said Santana, 36. “That doesn’t work anymore. Latinos want deeds.” Instead, outdated ideas were all Bass had. It started with her choice of chief campaign strategist: Julie Chavez Rodriguez, who was campaign manager for President Biden’s disastrous 2024 reelection bid and then Kamala Harris’ failed attempt to pick up the pieces. I quickly tuned out the one time Chavez Rodriguez described her vision for Latino outreach, which would have been revolutionary in L.A. two generations ago. While Bass' campaign mounted a vigorous media outreach effort in English and Spanish, her own attempts to court Latino voters kept backfiring. The crowd at the annual City Hall Mexican Independence Day celebration booed when Padilla, in a green outfit that matched Bass', hailed the mayor as "good." At Homegirl Cafe in Chinatown the morning before the election, customers largely ignored Bass while swarming gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra. She stood next to Becerra at the restaurant, only to have him later clarify to reporters that he wasn't endorsing anyone in the mayor's race. Michael Trujillo is a longtime political consultant who served as an unpaid advisor to a pro-Bass independent expenditure committee and has participated in the rise and struggles of the Eastside and San Fernando Valley machines. "It's going to take a long time" for L.A.’s Latino political establishment "to be reconstructed, and that’s ironic when you have Latinos in charge in Sacramento now," he said. But he predicted that Raman would bear her former opponents no ill will, because “they're going to give her a fair shot" — because what else can they do? The Raman era will undoubtedly boost a new generation of Latino leaders. But establishments don't fade away so easily — and insurgents don't automatically shun them. On Saturday, Raman attended a news conference to condemn the arrests of two people by federal immigration agents during an anti-ICE protest outside Adventist Health White Memorial Center. The mayor-elect shook the hands of state Sen. Maria Elena Durazo, SEIU California President David Huerta and Angelica Salas, executive director of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights of Los Angeles, all of whom endorsed Bass and recorded social media videos in support of the incumbent. When it was Raman's turn to speak, she led the crowd in chants of "ICE out of Boyle Heights" and praised Huerta, Durazo and Salas. Raman concluded by promising Angelenos in Spanish that she would "defend" immigrants. And then L.A.'s Latino political establishment did the only thing they could: They applauded.
news.summary: Almost all the city's Latino power brokers — politicians, nonprofit leaders, union activists, celebrities — bet big on longtime ally Karen Bass, only to now find themselves on the outside looking in.

news.title: The Democratic Party gained power across the country in the midterms. Now what?
news.text:
Two years ago, voters sent Democrats a message when they ousted them from power in Washington. At first glance, last week's midterm results sent a new one.

Democrats will enter the next Congress with one of the largest majorities in a generation, flipping dozens of House districts and at least seven Senate seats in mainly Trump-won communities. The party now controls a majority of governorships, and gained control of several additional state legislative chambers.

"I think one of the big surprises for me on Tuesday night was just how deep and wide our election results were," Democratic National Committee Chairman Ken Martin said in an interview with NPR. "This was the biggest election cycle for Democrats in the history of our party."

Martin, who has faced criticism from some inside the party throughout his term as chairman, said that the stunning Democratic victories across the country were the result of his party's focus on issues like affordability and ending the war in Iran.

He said the midterms were bigger than politics and bigger than party, and acknowledged the results were just as much about serving as a "massive repudiation of Donald Trump and the MAGA Trumpers and the Republican Party." "I think it's an admonition for Democrats, for sure: Now that we're in power, we have to deliver," he said. "But it was a complete message to Republicans. You had the ability to help us and you did nothing."

Blue tsunami in the South

With an expanded Congressional majority and a lame duck president, one of the frontlines for figuring out if the Democratic party's power will hold will be in the South, Martin said.

"Six of the 10 fastest growing parts of the country right now are below the Mason-Dixon line, and 40% of the U.S. population is going to live in the South after the next Census," he said. "As we go into 2032 and there's a realignment with the reapportionment, states like Minnesota, Michigan, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, New York, Rhode Island, Illinois and California are all going to lose electoral votes and congressional votes to the South."

Last week's midterms brought the region's power – especially with Black voters – more squarely into focus. Turbocharged Black voter turnout helped elect the country's first Black female governor in Georgia and may elect the first Black U.S. Senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction.

A slew of Republican-led states seeking to redraw House maps for partisan advantage backfired, as Democrats gained several seats across the region.

Georgia Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock said in an interview with NPR that Democratic victories in 2026 were a "proof of concept" that the South is central to the future of American politics.

"You saw a multiracial coalition of voters stand up on Tuesday night beyond anything I had even hoped for, and they offered a silent rebuke of where we are now," he told NPR. "It's now up to us to provide the leadership, even as we listen to people, and point the way forward into how we build an economy that works for everyday working families."

Warnock said Democrats' direction in the next two years should aim to serve as a cure for the last decade of Trump-dominated politics that has been defined more as top versus bottom rather than left versus right.

"Ordinary people have had their hopes dashed time and time again, cycle after cycle, across Republican and Democratic administrations," he said. "They've seen the widening chasm between the haves and the have nots."

He called the midterms a "moral moment" that will help determine what kind of nation America wants to be.

Looking ahead to 2028

In the early days after the 2026 elections, a look ahead to the 2028 presidential race finds both parties with the potential to see crowded fields of candidates in several new lanes reacting to signals sent by the electorate.

That includes Warnock, who will be up for reelection in 2028 and is among names floated as a presidential contender, along with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, California Rep. Ro Khanna, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, former Vice President Kamala Harris and others who have spent significant time in the South campaigning for other Democrats.

As new members of Congress descend on Washington for their orientations, competing visions for Democratic governance are on display with postmortem event panels called "What Worked" and "What Just Happened?" and event names like "What's Next" as party strategists argue online about which wing of the party was the most successful.

2026 victories also scramble the traditional map of swing states, Martin said, suggesting that Democrats would start off competitive in places like Florida and Texas and as favorites to win the White House.

"Texas is no longer a red state. It is a blue state. They didn't even go from red to purple to blue, which is a normal sort of progression," he said. "If Texas is now a blue state, and you look at Georgia and you look at other parts of the South, how do the Republicans get to 270 votes?"
news.summary: Voters handed Democrats the keys to power across the country and expect them to drive in a different direction. Party leaders are now trying to figure out which way to go.

news.title: Can the Republican Party survive Trump?
news.text:
There is a saying in politics: “Every election is fundamentally about the next one.” On November 3, the Republican Party suffered what some have labelled a near “extinction-level” loss in the 2026 midterms. With the results likely to offer an indication of what lies ahead in the next presidential election, what options do Republicans have for 2028? First, we need to understand why this latest “blue tsunami” occurred. The midterms were a rejection of Trump, not an endorsement of the Democrats.

Last Tuesday’s outcome reflected voters holding Trump responsible for economic disaster, huge increases in the cost of living, his failing war on Iran, and his catering to Israel. It is also a condemnation of the Trump family using the Oval Office to enrich themselves and their friends to an unprecedented degree.

Coming into the midterms, voters saw the Trump administration as corrupt and as having abandoned the populist grassroots that had helped him get elected in the first place. A bad economy, failed tariffs, and an unwanted war widened the gap between the MAGA loyalists – who remain loyal to Trump as a political figure – and the America First factions of the Republican Party, which remain loyal to the values that Trump had campaigned on but failed to deliver. It was the separation of these two groups, once seen as interchangeable, that ultimately destroyed the Trump coalition, which had brought Trump and the Republicans to power in Washington.

During the latest midterms, we witnessed many prominent voices in the conservative movement openly oppose Republican leaders. Popular conservatives such as Tucker Carlson and Marjorie Taylor Greene spoke out publicly against several Republican candidates, including Mike Rogers in Michigan and Ken Paxton in Texas. Former Trump supporter Nick Fuentes advocated for months for his followers to vote for Democrats. Their argument was that Trump had betrayed America First principles and could no longer be trusted. Many former grassroots Trump voters who had supported him because of his economic agenda and because he had said that he wanted “no more wars” had suffered greatly due to the increasing cost of living and job losses. In the end, Trump lost support among young voters, Hispanic and Latino voters, Black men, and suburban and independent voters.

These results put the Republican Party at a critical juncture, leaving many to wonder what vision the party will have in 2028. Should they focus more on the post-Trump era, leaving Trump behind, or double down on his original agenda and rebuild his coalition to stay relevant? There are two major forces at play here: Trump himself, as a powerful figure, and the Republican establishment that wants to regain control of the party and stay relevant. Many observers conflate these two forces, while others believe that Trump reinvented the party and became the establishment in the process. Both are wrong. While Trump is still the most powerful person in the Republican Party, and his broader political operation has many hundreds of millions of dollars to support his agenda, he was never the establishment.

The traditional Republican establishment includes institutional donor networks, former party leaders, Reaganite think tanks, and corporate lobbying groups that accepted Trump’s reign while he was delivering on judges and tax cuts, but never truly accepted his populist takeover. The midterm results have given a boost to the more traditional power structures to attempt, again, to “take their party back”. Both are powerful forces with influential bases. The establishment is counting particularly on the fact that the Trump coalition has weakened considerably and will be hard to regenerate. They think Trump is likely to focus his fundraising efforts on himself – in the form of building his presidential library – rather than helping new candidates. On the grassroots side, Republican voters feel betrayed after Trump’s poor handling of the Epstein scandal, unprecedented political profiteering and corruption allegations, and the war on Iran.

Since these midterms were a referendum on how unpopular Trump has become, this leaves the Republican Party with two primary options: rebuild the Trump coalition or prepare themselves for a post-Trump conservative party. The key question now is how Republican candidates can distance themselves from Trump while at the same time attempting to rebuild his winning voter base. Walking this tightrope will mean finding a way to bring MAGA and America First back together again. This may seem like an impossible task in the current political climate, but it is hard to imagine any other winning scenario.

There are many names already in play, with more likely to enter the field within the coming months. Vice President JD Vance seemed to be the heir apparent with the strongest prospects prior to the recent midterms. Vance is powerful in terms of his proximity to Trump and the support he can garner from MAGA and wealthy donors in the tech industry. He also has ties to the America First crowd. Turning Point USA endorsed him publicly a year ago. Tucker Carlson, with his large following, still supports Vance. On the other hand, Vance will have a hard time distancing himself from the Trump administration’s failures on the economy, immigration, and the war on Iran. Vance will have to walk a fine line, criticising Trump enough to distance himself from bad policies while not losing support from the hardcore MAGA base, which is likely to retaliate if it feels left behind. If Vance refuses to criticise Trump altogether, we will likely see a repeat of the Kamala Harris-Joe Biden scenario. One of Vance’s major weaknesses when it comes to electability is that he is not an establishment figure himself. He faced a difficult race for the US Senate in Ohio in 2022. Trump chose him in 2024 as his running mate due to his ties to the tech billionaires and to challenge the Republican establishment. These factors will complicate Vance’s journey within the 2028 field should the establishment start to regain its footing within Republican leadership circles.

The 2028 establishment favourite within the Trump administration is Marco Rubio. It will be easier for Rubio to distance himself from Trump’s economy, but he will have a harder time distancing himself from Trump’s foreign policy and the war. Rubio is well-liked within the establishment, neoconservative and traditional donor groups. However, he is not a MAGA favourite, nor is he seen as an America First choice. Rubio’s main problem is that he is many people’s second choice. Also, his relationship with controversial donors such as Miriam Adelson will be a significant obstacle for him, as will his views on Israeli influence in US politics.

When thinking about 2028, Ron DeSantis, the outgoing governor of Florida, is another strong player. He is positioning himself to lead the Republican Party after leaving office in January. DeSantis is widely credited with the only success that Republicans had in this brutal midterm. He also has close ties to pro-Israel donors in Florida and nationwide. However, his weak performance and failure in running a national campaign against Trump in 2024 have not been forgotten.

Besides these names, the field will likely have many other candidates, some of whom will represent the establishment, and more who will challenge both forces alike. While the midterms were a referendum on Trump’s lack of popularity, they were also a vote against the establishment. Many Republicans and conservatives will pick up on this momentum and attempt to act on it. In this camp, we could see people like Congressman Thomas Massie, a possible run by former Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, as well as complete outsiders who we don’t yet know. The determining factor, in my opinion, will be the Democrats. The Democrats’ strategy in managing the next two years will play a major role in the success or failure of the Republicans in 2028. In other words, 2028 is now the Democrats’ to lose.

Whether Democrats focus on anti-Trump retaliation or on rebuilding the economy and regaining voter trust will shape the Republicans’ ability to make a comeback. Retaliation will give Trump another chance at survival, but Democrats will have little incentive to shift their focus to anything other than anti-Trump rhetoric if they insist on keeping their current leadership as it is, without any radical shift against their donor class and wealthy elites.

Last Tuesday was a historic event the likes of which I have not seen in more than a decade on the campaign trail. This victory complicates the Democrats’ path to achieving real success for the American people, especially given Trump’s veto power. More than anything else, the future of the Republican Party will be determined by the ability of the Democrats to come up with their own strategy that is not dependent on being anti-Trump. In some ways, the Democrats need Trump – and need him to keep failing – in order for them to continue this winning streak. It will be up to Republicans to decide on their own whether they need him or not, and whether their party’s future will centre on the personality of one man.
news.summary: The party faces a battle for its future after the midterms, but Democrats may ultimately determine whether it recovers.

news.title: Midterms Survey Reveals Why Trump’s GOP Fell Short in 2022
news.text:
Less than a week after the Republican Party suffered its most severe electoral collapse since President Bill Clinton’s 1994 midterm defeat at the hands of Speaker Newt Gingrich’s Republican Revolution, political analysts are only beginning to piece together how President Donald Trump and his party went so badly off course.

Republicans losing control of Congress was significant. But Tuesday’s outcome went further: Democrats captured at least seven Republican-held Senate seats, giving the party its largest majority in the upper chamber in a decade. That result points to forces beyond a routine change in congressional control.

Vice President JD Vance began the search for answers Wednesday, suggesting that the Iran War had turned voters who supported the Trump-Vance ticket in 2024 into Democratic voters. Our data, however, does not support that conclusion.

Senator Ted Cruz likewise argued that “Republicans, Libertarians [and] Independents” had voted for Democrats, but he offered a different explanation. “Number one, cost of living, energy, and groceries,” he wrote, citing voter polling. “Corruption. Number two… [then] the cost of the Iran war…”

Both men captured part of the story. Neither provided the full explanation.

Cygnal, the polling firm I lead, launched its post-election midterm survey the day after the vote. Its findings offer a broader account of the forces behind the Republican Party’s historic defeat, the factors that turned a blue wave into a tsunami and the lessons both parties should take from the result.

About one in 12 people who voted for Trump in 2024 told us they did not vote Republican for Congress. That is close to the one in 10 identified in our final pre-election poll and represents roughly 4 percent of the entire electorate.

In a country where Republicans and Democrats are almost evenly matched, that shift alone was enough to change control of the House of Representatives.

Republican voters also explained their decisions in their own words. Broken promises, dishonesty and corruption topped the list, followed by weak candidates, the Iran war and high prices. Only about one in eight cited Trump, his family or his administration as the reason they left the party.

“They betrayed every promise,” wrote a lifelong Republican Millennial man from the Midwest. “Never voted for any Democrat ever until now. We gave them [the] president and full Congress and [they] did nothing.”

An older Republican voter put it even more plainly: “Trump said imagine me on the ballot. I did, and for the first time since 1972, I voted Democrat.”

An Independent voter offered this assessment in the Cygnal survey: “[Republicans] keep presenting worse and worse candidates. It’s like they’re actively trying to lose with [these] clowns.”

Trump’s net favorability rating among voters was an abysmal minus 25. Republicans in Congress fared no better, recording a minus 29, while Democrats in Congress were viewed less negatively, at minus 9.

When asked who bore the greatest responsibility for the Republican loss of Congress, 43 percent pointed to Trump, 21 percent cited high prices and 13 percent blamed the Iran war.

The issues Republicans had expected to drive their supporters to the polls also faded from the campaign conversation.

Only 12 percent identified immigration as their primary reason for voting. Inflation, at 20 percent, threats to democracy, at 21 percent, and political corruption, at 20 percent, were the leading concerns among midterm voters.

Gas prices and the Iran war were among the issues voters most remembered seeing in campaign advertisements. Yet just 2 percent named gas prices and 4 percent named the Iran war as their main reason for voting.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT: Man Accused of Holding Teen in Basement, Forcing Brace Removal

The range of voter concerns makes it difficult to accept Vance’s argument that the Iran war explains the scale of the Republican defeat. His broader point about Republican voters abandoning their party, however, appears to be supported by the data.

One in five voters said they had seriously or somewhat considered choosing the other party’s candidate before making a final decision. There were many potential openings, but they led almost entirely in one direction: toward the Democrats.

Cross-party voting, in which supporters of one party choose the opposing party’s candidates, was effectively a one-way street this election. In our final poll, only 1 percent of Democrats said they planned to vote Republican.

Did Republican voters who crossed the aisle turn a wave into a tsunami? In part, yes. But the larger story may involve the Republicans who never made it to the polls.

In my final pre-election analysis, published by Our News Outlet less than a week before voting began, I identified a group I called the “Fatalists.” These Republican-leaning voters expected Democrats to win.

Among the Fatalists who ultimately voted, one described the result as “disappointed but not surprised.” Another said: “Predictable. You knew it was going to happen.”

Fatalists accounted for 9 percent of voters in Cygnal’s final poll, and fewer than half were highly motivated to vote. They correctly anticipated the outcome—and I suspect some helped bring it about.

Polling has an unavoidable limitation: people who stay home are, by definition, absent from surveys of voters. Even so, the size of the gap they leave behind can be measured.

In our post-election survey, 49 percent of respondents said they had voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, compared with 44 percent who said they had voted for Donald Trump. In reality, Trump won the national popular vote in 2024 by roughly 1.5 points. That 6.5-point difference reflects large numbers of Trump voters who stayed home, as well as some respondents who no longer acknowledge having voted for him in 2024.

A survey cannot determine the precise size of those two groups. My expectation, however, is that final voting data released next year will show that many Republican-leaning Americans who rarely voted but turned out for Trump in 2024 did not participate in 2026.

There is, finally, a potential bright spot for Republicans—and a warning for Democrats.

The Republican voters who defected this year were not ideological converts. The survey’s findings point consistently toward the same advice for the party’s future.

We asked voters what Republicans should do to improve their chances in future elections. The leading responses were to listen to ordinary people, cited by 21 percent; be honest and address corruption, 12 percent; reduce prices and repair the economy, 12 percent; and move away from hatred and division, 11 percent.

Nine percent said Republicans should break with Trump and MAGA, while 3 percent said they should remain aligned with them.

“Listen to the average person, and quit telling us everything is wonderful,” wrote one strongly Republican voter. “It’s not for us Seniors.” Another offered a simpler message: “When elected do what you say you’re going to do.”

A majority of voters—52 percent—want the new Congress to work with Trump, even if that requires compromise. Forty percent want Congress to serve as a check on him, and one-third of voters cannot identify the leader of the Democratic Party.

Put simply, the tsunami was not the result of a mass ideological conversion. It was a verdict delivered by Republicans who crossed over and by an as-yet-unknown number who chose not to vote. The first group can be won back: lower prices, honor commitments and nominate stronger candidates. The second will be more difficult to reach because persuasion cannot work on people who have already decided that voting is pointless.

Republicans have two years to begin rebuilding trust with voters who have just told them, in unmistakable terms, what they want.

news.title: CNN’s Van Jones Exposes the Democrats’ ‘Affordability’ Propaganda Machine
news.text:
In the wake of the Democrats’ midterm wins, CNN’s Van Jones and Kaitlan Collins reveled in one of the more successful deceptive strategies the left used to overwhelm Republicans on economic issues like “affordability.”

Jones admitted that the economy really isn’t as bad as portrayed, and that the Democrats knew this (surprise!), but rather than simply program their candidates and campaigns with duplicitous messaging, they took it several steps further. And the Republicans never figured it out.

Jones told Collins how the Democrats discreetly organized tens of thousands of people to serve as chartered trolls as part of the “American Accountability Network.” Jones did not make clear whether these people were compensated or not.

"The Republicans never figured out what we were doing," Jones said in-studio to a smiling Collins. "There's something called the American Accountability Network (AAN), tens of thousands of online humans, not bots, coordinated to make the affordability message a winning message online. 32.5 million people hit on Instagram every day. 88.8 million hit on Twitter, X, every single day. And 185 million Facebook hits every single day. And they never figured it out."

"The Republicans could not understand it wasn't bots. It was actual human beings," he said.

Oil crashed the day after Democrats took Congress. Then Van Jones went on CNN and admitted the quiet part out loud. The day after the election, Brent crude fell 8.7% in a single day. WTI fell 13% on the week. Worst week for oil since COVID. Nothing about the war changed overnight. Only the election ended. And it is still falling this morning. WTI is down near $87 a barrel. Tankers are still getting hit near the Strait of Hormuz. But the fear is gone, right on schedule. The official story is that traders think a Democrat Congress will force Trump to end the Iran war. Maybe. Hold that thought. Because then Van Jones went on CNN and bragged about how they did it. His exact words: 'The Republicans never figured out what we were doing.' Jones said Democrats ran something called the American Accountability Network. Tens of thousands of real people. Not bots. Coordinated to post the same message, everywhere, every day. And the message never changed. Everything is unaffordable. Gas costs too much. And it is all the Republicans' fault. Jones said they tied kitchen table pain to Democrats on a positive and Republicans on a negative. The scale he claimed: 32.5 million hits a day on Instagram. 88.8 million on X. 185 million on Facebook. That is not a campaign. That is a flood. And it was aimed at your gas tank. This was not some random group either. The network's own partner list includes the DNC, the DCCC, the DSCC, MoveOn, the AFL-CIO and the SEIU. The whole machine, working one message. So here is the question people are asking now. If the crisis was real, why did oil fall off a cliff the morning after the votes were counted? Inventories actually went down that week. Less oil sitting around usually means higher prices. Prices crashed anyway. They did not win on policy. They won on volume. I could even predict how these people would respond if I posted on certain topics, like affordability, the economy, and the fakeness of Texas Senator-elect James Talarico.

It’s a wonder that the Republicans did not see this and have an answer for it.

According to the American Accountability Network’s (AAN’s) website, some of the names on its long list of past clients include AFL-CIO, AFSCME, American Federation of Teachers, DCCC, Human Rights Campaign, League of Conservation Voters, MoveOn, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, Joe Biden, SEIU, Sen. Jon Ossoff, Kamala Harris, and VoteVets.

In his victory celebration on the CNN set, Jones told Collins that the end result of the propaganda campaign was, “everywhere you go, people are talking about affordability.”

He added that Democrats were having trouble getting any “traction” on culture war issues, but thanks to the AAN, the left “figured out how to get around all that.”

So, it’s not just all the door knocking that was done which was amazing. It’s not just our amazing candidate quality. We had something called the American Accountability Network.Don’t get mad at me, I was given permission to reveal this. They never figured it out and that network is going to continue to push for kitchen table issues and hold our democratic lawmakers accountable, Jones added.

Collins found all of this “fascinating.” Of course, it’s fascinating when Democrats do it, but if Republicans did it, it would be criminal to Collins and her ilk.

In my work in crisis and issues management, I’ve come up against organizations like the AAN and their clients. While I can’t speak to how the AAN waged this specific campaign, to give you a little inside baseball, here’s how they typically operate.

Many compensate their “volunteer” trolls with stringer or freelancer cash, or sometimes with gift cards. The trolls are given metric goals to hit to make more money or win prizes like those gift cards. So, if you’re one of the trolls they recruit, the more active you are at “engaging” with your opponents and getting clicks and shares, the more money you make.

The trolls are trained and given key messaging documents. They may role-play with each other to practice techniques for baiting conservatives into debating them online. Their goal is to drive you crazy and, in the process, create the perception that you’re the unhinged side of the debate, in this case, on the affordability issue.

Their audience is people who are scrolling TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, and X.

It’s not hard for them to find their army of trolls. Since Democrats own the labor unions, teachers’ unions, Antifa types, and professional agitator sector, all they have to do is put the word out, and the would-be trolls come calling.

Troll farms and their organizers have sophisticated monitoring systems in place so that they are alerted whenever a social media user posts one of the keywords they are watching for. If you use one of their keywords, as soon as your post pops up on their screen, they attack. Sometimes in swarms.

Over the years, one type of post I’ve made has always brought the paid trolls out of the woodwork. Whenever I’ve seen a fake protest, I have posted something to the effect of, “Who’s paying for this?”

That’s like throwing red meat into a hyena’s cage. “No one is paying for it!” is the message from the mob. The attacks get personal real quick.

Another technique these firms like to use is something they used to call a “Twitter storm.” That’s a pre-planned, scheduled attack on an unsuspecting target. One telltale sign of a Twitter storm is when you see the term “recently discovered social media posts.” Usually, that’s a pre-planned social media storm. They’ve been sitting on those posts for a long time, most likely, and they already have the campaign ready to take those posts out of context and smear the poster. This is how, overnight, you start hearing about a particular celebrity or politician who didn’t bow to the left’s sacred cows on cue.

Speaking of sacred cows, one example was in the waning days of the Abdul El-Sayed campaign. Republicans attacked the now-Senator-elect for refusing to disavow the terrorist Muslim Brotherhood.

While I can’t know whether the AAN was involved with this, I did see the obvious pattern of paid trolls trying to reframe the issue on social media as MAGA attacking El-Sayed for how he practices his faith. I pointed this out on October 20.

That was when I wrote about a “spontaneous” outbreak of posts that supposedly came from authentic Christians with no political agenda. They all featured the term “As a Christian,” just before launching into a defense of El-Sayed amid his refusal to distance himself from radical Islam.

The two-pronged strategy in this op is first to shift the focus away from El-Sayed’s consistent association with and support of radical Islamic figures and organizations, and to reframe it all as El-Sayed being a man of faith, just like President John Fitzgerald Kennedy was a misunderstood Catholic when he ran for president, I wrote.

On October 16, I wrote about the same sort of propaganda on social media, but with a different term. This time, the campaign was built around the term “Lifelong Republican.”

Apparently, the term is performing quite well in Democrat research when coupled with related content on how said 'lifelong Republican' is dissatisfied with President Donald Trump, his administration, and Republicans in general. By 'performing quite well,' I mean it’s effectively working to give Republicans pause and perhaps influence them to give up on voting in the midterms, I wrote.

Even now, don’t think the propaganda has stopped. You’re being bombarded with supposedly rational explanations as to why the Democrats won in so many places where they had never won before.

To be sure, the propaganda techniques the Democrats are still using are powerful. They likely swayed no small number of independents and squishy Republican voters. But in cases where other shenanigans are at play, that’s where the Democrats are still on the offensive, attacking anyone who might question the results and calling their targets “conspiracy theorists.”

If you think the election is over, it’s not. The campaign now is to kill any attempts to re-examine the midterm results and suspicious activities, and to set the stage to intimidate anyone who might try to hold the new Democrat majorities in Congress and the Senate to account.

news.title: Jeffries Says Minimum Wage Must ‘Be Raised’—Map Shows States at $7.25
news.text: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said the federal minimum wage “needs to be raised” on Monday after Democrats retook control of the House of Representatives and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections. Jeffries, a New York Democrat who is considered the frontrunner to become the next House speaker, was asked whether Democrats would now be interested in passing a minimum wage increase once they control Congress in January. The federal minimum wage remains $7.25 per hour, and it was last raised in 2009. Although many states have implemented higher wages, 20 others have not done so. “It’s a conversation that I look forward to having with not simply the members of the House Democratic caucus, but with the Senate as well, to see what is possible,” Jeffries said. “It certainly needs to be increased. It’s a disgrace that the minimum wage hasn’t been raised in 20 years and is currently $7.25 per hour.” A minimum wage increase would still need some bipartisan support. While it could pass the House, where Democrats have won 254 seats with 18 races to be called, the Senate remains a tougher lift. Democrats will control anywhere between 54 and 56 Senate seats, depending on the outcome in Alaska and Mississippi, but that is still not enough to clear the filibuster, so some Republicans would need to vote to raise the wage, as well. Whether President Donald Trump, who signaled some openness to raise the wage after his 2024 victory, would sign it into law also remains an open question. Newsweek reached out to the White House for comment via email. Twenty States Use Federal Minimum Wage In total, 20 states still use the federal $7.25 minimum wage, according to data from the Department of Labor. Those states include: Of those states, 19 voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential race. New Hampshire is the only state won by former Vice President Kamala Harris that does not have its own, higher minimum wage. Washington is the state with the highest minimum wage at $17.13 per hour. Several Republican-run states have higher minimum wages. The minimum wage in Florida, Missouri and Nebraska is $15 per hour. Several states including Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina and Tennessee all have no state minimum wage, so the federal minimum wage applies. Georgia and Wyoming both have minimum wages of $5.15 per hour, so the federal minimum applies there, as well. Many of the states that gave Democrats some of their biggest wins last week still have $7.25 minimum wages. That includes Georgia and Texas, where Democrats swept most statewide races, as well as South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews flipped a Senate seat. Affordability Central to Midterms Jeffries’ comments come on the heels of an election defined by the affordability issue. Voters, polls found, were chiefly concerned by the cost of living, and Democrats made addressing affordability a cornerstone of their pitch to take back Congress. Trump also emphasized affordability during his 2024 presidential run, and the issue was seen as what helped propel him back into the White House. Raising the minimum wage is a popular position, according to a recent YouGov poll, which found that 68 percent of Americans support raising it to $15 per hour and 73 percent would support raising it to $12 per hour. It surveyed 1,122 adults from August 17 to 20 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.1 percentage points. Democrats like Scott Colom, who has a narrow lead in the uncalled Mississippi Senate race, voiced support for raising the wage on the campaign trail. “The federal minimum wage is still $7.25. Same as it was over 25 years ago. Cindy High Prices has voted against raising it while voting to give herself a raise. That’s corrupt. Mississippi deserves better, and this November, we’re going in a new direction,” he wrote in a September 15 X post. Trump Said He Would ‘Consider’ Minimum Wage Increase Trump signaled some openness to raising the minimum wage in a December 2024 interview with NBC News, saying the current wage is “a very low number,” but that raising the wage could lead to higher prices. “But there is a level at which you could do it, absolutely,” he said. He said businesses are “thriving” because of the minimum wage, but that raising it “too much” is bad for business. “I would consider it. I want to speak to the governors,” he said. “The other thing that is very complicated about minimum wage is that places are so different. Mississippi and Alabama, great places, are very different than New York or California in terms of the cost of living or other things. It would be nice to have just a minimum wage for the whole country, but it wouldn’t work.” Bernie Sanders Called for $20 Minimum Wage After Midterms Progressives such as Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, are calling for more significant wage increases. In a post-midterm address posted to YouTube, he said the minimum wage is a “starvation wage” that “must change.” “Democrats must raise it to a living wage of at least $20 per hour and make it easier for workers to form unions by passing the PRO Act,” he said. “A job must lift people out of poverty, not keep them in it.” Minimum Wage Hike Efforts Have Stalled There have been efforts in Congress to address the federal minimum wage, but those attempts have stalled over the years. The Living Wage for All Act, introduced by Senator Chris Murphy of Connecticut and Representative Delia Ramirez of Illinois, both Democrats, calls for a federal minimum wage of $25 per hour. Murphy said during a press conference earlier this year that the minimum wage “should be a living wage.” “This is the most powerful, the most affluent, the wealthiest country in the world,” he said. “There is no reason that somebody should go to work full time in this country and not be able to pay their bills. There is no excuse for it.” Another bill, the Raise the Wage Act of 2021, would have raised the federal minimum wage to $15 per hour, but it did not pass Congress to become law.
news.summary: The minimum wage is still $7.25 per hour in 20 states, nearly all of which backed President Donald Trump in the 2024 election.
