news.title: A Capitol Hill vibe shift: From the Politics Desk
news.text: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into the vibe shift on Capitol Hill with lawmakers returning to Washington for the first time since the midterm elections. Plus, Joelle Gross zeroes in on the Democratic candidates who made the furthest inroads with President Donald Trump’s voters. — Adam Wollner A blue tsunami empowers Democrats as Congress returns to Washington Analysis by Sahil Kapur The vibes are different on Capitol Hill, with Republicans still shell-shocked by the magnitude of last week’s electoral thumping as they return to Washington as lame ducks with a lengthy to-do list. Outstanding items include: Passing a government funding bill by the Dec. 11 deadline to prevent a shutdown.Passing the annual National Defense Authorization Act.Passing a farm bill for agriculture and food-assistance policy.Deciding whether — and how — to renew FISA Section 702 warrantless surveillance.Figuring out a permitting reform deal to streamline construction projects.Figuring out whether to pass or abandon a college sports bill.Reviewing President Donald Trump’s nominees in the Senate.Considering a House resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, led by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky. Democrats feel empowered by their far-reaching midterm victories, as they made deep incursions into red-leaning territory amid a voter backlash to Trump. Some say that their mandate includes ending the Iran war and that lawmakers shouldn’t pass any government funding bill without cutting off money for Trump to continue the war without congressional approval. “I believe we would abdicate our responsibility if we voted to provide billions of additional dollars for President Trump’s war of choice in Iran,” Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., a moderate, wrote in a letter to colleagues Saturday. “We must refuse to invoke cloture on any package that includes another cent for his war.” Meanwhile, a small group of Republicans is pushing to delay tomorrow’s closed-door meeting to pick their leadership team for the next two years. The top three GOP senators — John Thune of South Dakota, John Barrasso of Wyoming and Tom Cotton of Arkansas — are favored to hold their positions in the minority, but not without some pushback. “A week ago, we had the worst election result in decades. We need a discussion about what went wrong, how we fix it, what we stand for, and how our agenda must focus on the concerns of the American people,” Sen. David McCormick, R-Pa., who rarely steps out of line with GOP leadership, said in a statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward,” he added. There is no internal consensus yet among Republicans about why they lost so decisively, and many of them are reluctant to point fingers at Trump, even though the results and exit polls overwhelmingly indicate voters were delivering a rebuke of him. Thune said the election gives the GOP an “opportunity to reflect on what we as a party need to do better.” The big question for Trump and Republicans is how much they’re willing to compromise over the next six weeks, while they retain their maximum leverage, to achieve some of their year-end goals. Come Jan. 3, Democrats are poised to take power on Capitol Hill with some of the biggest majorities here since 2009. How exit poll data explains the millions of Trump voters who went blue, in maps and charts By Joelle Gross Millions of Americans who voted for President Donald Trump backed Democrats in last week’s midterm elections — that much is clear from the vote counts. But to understand why, it helps to drill down into the exit polls. Voters turned away from Trump and the Republicans out of deep frustration over the economy and concerns about the state of American democracy, an analysis of the NBC News Exit Poll data found. Democrats re-energized young and Latino voters, among other groups, fueling a historic takeover of Congress and grabbing Senate seats in states that had seemed tattooed red. Tuesday’s Democratic success came not only by mobilizing the party’s base. Senate candidates from Texas to South Carolina to New Hampshire swayed former Trump voters. In some states, percentages of Trump voters turning out for Democrats reached double digits. About 13% of voters who chose Trump in 2024 voted for Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia this year, the exit poll suggests. James Talarico in Texas and Mark Warner in Virginia drew 11%. Nationally, around 7% of former Trump voters opted for Democratic candidates in House elections. By comparison, 2% of those who voted for Kamala Harris split for Republican House candidates. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.
news.summary: In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into the vibe shift on Capitol Hill with lawmakers returning to Washington for the first time since the midterm elections.

news.title: Harry Enten Can't Think Of A More 'Tone Deaf' Choice For Trump's Top Staffer — And Has The Stats To Prove It
news.text:
If President Donald Trump wants to win back voters who ditched Republicans for Democrats this midterms, CNN’s data analyst Harry Enten thinks he sure tapped the wrong person to be the next White House chief of staff.

The stat-savvy politico was wowed that the president picked anti-immigration hardliner Stephen Miller for the post fresh on the heels of the GOP losing a huge share of Latino voters in last week’s election.

“Gosh, how tone deaf is this White House? You get the results from last week, and then you make Stephen Miller chief of staff,” Enten said on Monday’s episode of “NewsCentral.” “What are they? They are in another planet. They’re in another universe that we’re talking about.”

“I mean, just look at these shifts,” he said, pulling up a chart on “who Latinos trust more on immigration” that showed Trump three points up on Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 while Democrats now land at +21.

Enten highlighted numbers from a selection of districts with large Latino communities that spanned from Texas to New Jersey as he added, “We saw it across the political map no matter what state, no matter what region you were in.”

“What the heck is going on out there?” Enten asked of Miller’s appointment.

As White House deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser during Trump’s second term, Miller has been behind many of the most aggressive policies shaping the administration’s crackdown on immigrants.

Before Trump even took office, Miller oversaw a team drafting executive orders aimed at ending birthright citizenship and designating of drug cartels as foreign terrorist organizations.

In the past two years, he’s also pushed for the dramatic ramp up in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Border Patrol operations, daily arrest quotas, implementing the Alien Enemies Act to bypass due process, and restricting the ways asylum-seekers and refugees can stay in and enter the U.S.

news.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is likely to keep his job for now, say prediction markets
news.text:
One event contract on Kalshi asking when Huang will leave as Nvidia’s CEO has drawn more than $266,000 in trading volume. Traders put the probability of his departure before January 2029 at 54%, compared with 52% before January 2028 and 33% before July 2027. A separate Kalshi market has drawn roughly $2,500 in trading volume, with traders putting the probability that Huang will testify before Congress by next January at 46%, rising to 79% by next July.

Polymarket has also listed a market on when Huang’s resignation or removal as CEO will be announced, drawing more than $305,000 in trading volume. Traders put the probability of an announcement by year-end at 16%, rising to 22% by the end of March 2027.

Meanwhile, Polymarket is also offering wagers about Huang’s personal life. There are currently around $159,000 of bets on the probability of a divorce by March 2027, with current odds at 23%.

The event contracts come a day after Nvidia announced an investigation into Huang, who acknowledged to the company’s board that he had an intimate relationship with a business executive whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly identified as a Chinese spy. Nvidia shares have fallen nearly 10% since Monday morning.

With Huang’s future uncertain, traders have turned the corporate scandal into a running forecast of what could happen next, much as they do with other unfolding news.

These platforms allow users to trade on outcomes across sports, politics, and even the weather, with prices reflecting traders’ expectations of how events will unfold. They drew substantial attention during last week’s midterm elections, when traders favored Democrats to win control of both chambers of Congress.

The midterm results bolstered prediction markets’ reputation as forecasting tools. The platforms rose to prominence during the 2024 presidential election, when traders favored Donald Trump to win while polls showed a close race between him and Democratic candidate Kamala Harris.

But the platforms’ forecasts have not always matched the results. While prediction markets broadly anticipated Democratic gains in the midterms, they favored Republicans in the Texas governor’s race and South Carolina’s Senate race, both of which Democrats ultimately won.

An earlier surprise in Brazil’s presidential election also raised questions about the platforms’ forecasting accuracy.
news.summary: A Polymarket contract on when Huang will resign or be removed as Nvidia CEO has drawn nearly $300,000 in trading volume.

news.title: Kamala Harris Finishes 16th With Under 1% In Progressive 2028 Straw Poll
news.text:
Authored by AG News Staff via American Greatness,

Former Vice President Kamala Harris drew just 0.6 percent in a 2028 presidential straw poll at a gathering of progressive activists, finishing 16th, the New York Post reported.

The informal vote was held this weekend at Crooked Con, a left-wing convention organized by Crooked Media, a company founded by Obama administration alumni. About 1,000 votes were cast, and the poll was not a scientific survey.

Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, fresh off his reelection win over Republican Rep. Mike Collins, led the field with 38 percent. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York was second at 17 percent, followed by former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 14 percent.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro each received 4 percent. Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore drew 3 percent, and California Gov. Gavin Newsom took 2.3 percent. Harris tied with Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin.

The result is a stunning fall for Harris, the party's 2024 nominee, who led by double digits in nearly every 2028 Democratic primary poll before the midterms. She still leads the RealClearPolitics average at 21.8 percent, ahead of Newsom at 13.5 percent, with Ossoff in fifth at 10.8 percent.

[ZH: Polymarket shows her at the bottom of the pile, with Newsom losing significant ground as Ossoff takes off...]

Ossoff himself has tried to tamp down talk of a White House run. Asked in a debate last month whether he would serve a full six-year Senate term, he said, "Yes, I will." He has also said, "I have zero interest in running for president. I'm running for Senate."

Ossoff's appeal to activists is notable given his record. He has opposed Medicare for All, the Green New Deal, calls to abolish ICE and efforts to expand the Supreme Court.

news.title: Polling expert breaks down young men’s midterm shift to Democrats
news.text:
John Della Volpe, director of polling at Harvard Kennedy School’s Institute of Politics, joined “Morning Joe” to discuss the “whiplash” young men delivered Republicans on Election Day by shifting their support to Democrats — and what he believes the party must do to hold on to the key demographic in 2028.

According to preliminary voter data, 62% of men under 30 voted for Democrats in the midterms, compared with 36% who backed Republicans. That marks a sharp shift from 2024, when young men supported Donald Trump over Kamala Harris, 55% to 41%.

“No group switched more than young men in the entire electorate,” Della Volpe said Monday morning. And, as he explained, that shift crossed educational lines. “Younger men without a college degree are about as likely to support Democrats as young men with a college degree,” he said.

Despite young men helping to return Trump to the White House in 2024, their optimism about his presidency began to fade, he said, when Trump started talking about tariffs and taxes.

Della Volpe said young men’s support comes down to “which party understands me, and which party delivers for me.” That, he said, was “the message and the rebuke” that many Americans, particularly younger men, sent to the Republican Party last week.

Still, he cautioned Democrats against taking young men’s support for granted. Their allegiance, he said, may be more fluid than either party once assumed. “We thought Democrats would have younger people for a generation, Republicans for a generation. Of course, that’s not true,” he explained.

Della Volpe outlined four “keys” he believes will determine which party can win young men in the next election: listening to them and understanding their aspirations; making the economic case in concrete terms, including the costs of raising a family, buying a home and saving for education; addressing corruption, including calls to ban congressional stock trading; and speaking to the broader “aspirations of their generation.”

Ultimately, he said, the message comes down to two issues that are two sides of the same coin: “cost of living and corruption.”

“Deliver on it,” he advised Democrats.

You can watch Della Volpe’s full analysis in the clip at the top of the page.

news.text:
President Donald Trump announced on Friday that Stephen Miller — one of his and the MAGA movement's most stalwart defenders — would be replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.

A White House official told Blaze News that "with this new appointment, the White House will be an extremely fine-tuned machine that will implement the President’s policies and represent the populist movement he created with MAGA."

news.title: Trump Questions Midterm Election Results Over 'Wrong' Polls Amid Blue Wave
news.text: President Donald Trump questioned the results of the 2026 midterm elections in a post on Truth Social on Monday, asking how the polls could have been “so wrong” as the Republican Party continued grappling with major losses in the House of Representatives and Senate. One expert Newsweek spoke with, however, defended the polls, saying they "underestimated magnitude but got the vector right." Polls underestimated Democrats by several points in the midterms, shattering the narrative that Republicans are routinely underestimated. RealClearPolitics’ generic ballot average showed Democrats up 8.8 points over Republicans, but Democrats ended up winning by 13 points, according to data from The New York Times as of Monday morning, when some votes were yet to be counted. That had major implications for both parties. Although Democrats were seen as favorites to flip control of the House, and the Senate was seen as competitive, Democrats are poised to win both chambers easily, with more than 250 seats in the House and at least 54 seats in the Senate, with several seats uncalled. Trump on Monday took to Truth Social, questioning if anyone believes the election was “honest.” “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!” he wrote. Polling error may come down to the estimates of who is considered a “likely voter,” a group that has been changing, Grant Davis Reeher, professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek. “In defense of the polls, they did correctly show and predict that races one would have thought would not be particularly competitive were in fact extremely competitive,” he said. “They underestimated magnitude but got the vector right. And there may have been some late-breaking voters, in terms of turnout and in terms of vote choice, who the polls simply missed through no fault of their own.” As for future elections, Reeher said he believes Republicans still have around 43 percent of the vote “baked in.” “Unless they field a really bad candidate, a presidential election year should generate its own enthusiasm,” he said. “And a lot depends of course on what Democrats do with this victory, in terms of their presidential own sweepstakes.” Newsweek reached out to the Democratic and Republican national committees for comment via email. How Wrong Were Polls in Key Senate Races? Polling across the board underestimated Democrats in key Senate races. The largest polling miss was in Texas, where polling showed Democratic Senator-elect James Talarico with a slight edge over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton—but Talarico ended up winning by double digits. RCP’s average gave Talarico a 2.6-point lead, but he won by 12.1 points—a polling miss of more than 9 points. Georgia also saw a 9-point polling miss. Senator Jon Ossoff led by an average of 8.4 points, per RCP, but was on track to win by 18 points. In South Carolina, polling gave Senator Darline Graham a 2.6-point lead, but she was on track to lose to Democratic Senator-elect Annie Andrews by 4.5 points. Here is a look at how polls missed in 11 key Senate races. Republicans Banked on Pro-GOP Polling Error In the final stretch of the campaign, Republicans said they believed polling was inaccurate and were banking on a pro-Republican polling error. House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, said during an interview on Fox News’ The Ingraham Angle that polls were “grossly underestimating Republican enthusiasm.” “I think it’s even further off this time because more and more Republicans are unwilling to participate in these surveys. They don’t want to give their information to someone on the phone. They don’t play along. They’re calling it the partisan nonresponse bias,” he said. Nate Silver wrote in an October 20 Substack post that pollsters are “acutely aware” of the challenge that Republicans are less likely to participate in polls and have a “variety of tactics and techniques to combat it.” “They can match to Census Bureau demographics, or they can anchor to the past reported vote. Or there might be approaches that are a little bit more subjective: for instance, playing around with assumptions in likely voter models. Pollsters might herd or refuse to publish results they deem too far out of consensus; it’s happened before in the U.S. and abroad,” he wrote. Polling Hasn’t Always Underestimated Republicans While it is true that Republicans have been underestimated in polls during several recent elections, that is not always the case. Polling error is not replicated from cycle to cycle. Pro-Republican polling errors have been most pronounced during presidential years when Trump was on the ballot. In 2018, the generic ballot polling error also favored Democrats, though by a less dramatic margin. RCP had Democrats up 7.3 points in their final average; they ended up winning by 8.4 points. Polling was fairly accurate in 2022. Republicans led the generic ballot by 2.5 points, according to RCP, and went on to win by 2.8 points. Republicans have modestly overperformed their polling in recent presidential races, though the difference has only been a few points. In 2024, polling was only a few points off. RCP’s average had former Vice President Kamala Harris up only 0.1 points over Trump, who carried the national popular vote by 1.5 points. In 2020, RCP had former President Joe Biden up 7.2 points in the polls; he ended up winning by 4.5 points, and by even narrower margins in key swing states. RCP had former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton up 3.2 points in 2016. She ended up winning the popular vote by just over 2 points, while losing the Electoral College. What Has Donald Trump Said About Midterm Results? Trump's latest comments mark a shift from his response on election night. “I am absolutely willing to accept those results,” Trump told the New York Times on election night. “We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out.” In other election-night remarks, Trump sought to distance himself from the Republican defeat, writing on Truth Social: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Prior to the midterms, the president told reporters he would accept the results if they were "honest elections." On Sunday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that the U.S. "took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Polls were wrong again in this year's midterms. Unlike the last few cycles, however, Democrats benefited from that polling error.

news.title: Illinois voters pass proposals formally objecting to state anti-BDS law
news.text: Voters in eight municipalities in Illinois approved ballot measures last week, registering formal objections to the state's law barring state pension investments in companies that boycott Israel.The ballot measures will have no effect on state policy. But pro-Palestinian groups are celebrating the wins as demonstrations of shifting public opinion against the law, first signed in 2015 to oppose the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions movement.The village of Oak Park and the townships of Champaign, Cunningham, DuPage, Kickapoo, Medina, Normal and Peoria all approved similarly worded ballot measures that urge the state to repeal its anti-BDS law or support specific state legislation that would do so. According to unofficial tallies, 65% of voters in Oak Park, a Chicago suburb whose local Jewish population mounted a sustained objection to the referendum, approved the measure there.Jewish groups including the Jewish United Fund, Chicago's federation arm, had campaigned against the ballot measure. The Illinois law, championed by JUF when it was first passed, was the first of what has become dozens of state anti-BDS laws in the country. First Amendment groups have challenged the laws.Those opposed to the referendum didn't have enough time, JUF says“We would have much preferred a victory,” Dan Goldwin, chief public affairs officer for JUF, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency on Monday. Yet Goldwin pointed out that Oak Park voters had approved the measure by smaller margins than their votes for top Democratic candidates, including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and former presidential candidate Kamala Harris.“Once people began to be exposed to the meaning of what the referendum was about, they moved against it. We just didn't have enough time,” he said. Some members of the Oak Park opposition had engaged in a drawn-out fight over the eligibility of the signatures the ballot measure activists had gathered. That time, Goldwin theorized, “was probably time better spent convincing people to vote against it.”Separately, voters in Bloomington Township approved a measure stating that the federal government should “ban the transfer of weapons to any country that is a dictatorship, apartheid state or major violator of human rights.” The ballot language did not mention Israel, but pro-Palestinian activists have long maintained that Israel commits apartheid and that the US should halt weapons sales to the country.Jewish figures express concern over measureLocal Jewish figures have said the campaign troubled them.“It felt like it was a local chapter of a global movement to destroy the world's only Jewish state, and I felt it personally and acutely,” Rabbi Adir Glick of Conservative Temple Har Zion in River Forest, which borders Oak Park, told the Wednesday Journal of Oak Park and River Forest about the campaign. “I know people who lost friendships in the last few months, and difficult moments with neighbors and colleagues, but it also galvanized our Jewish community.” Goldwin said the measures' passage wouldn't change JUF's own strategy opposing the repeal of the anti-BDS law at the state level. He noted that ballot measure activists, with the exception of Oak Park, largely didn't target municipalities with large Jewish communities. In his view, those seeking the repeal of the law “are still a significant minority.”The BDS movement had a more significant policy victory on election night with the passage of a binding ballot referendum in Providence, Rhode Island, to divest that city from “foreign countries conducting ethnic cleansing, apartheid, illegal military occupation, or genocide.” Proponents and opponents of the measure alike have said they believe the language and parameters of the question will include Israel.
news.author: Andrew Lapin/jta

news.title: Jan. 6 should follow Trump 'to his grave,' Biden says in new memoir
news.text:
Former President Joseph Biden claims his successor was desperate to hang on to power after losing the 2020 election, saying, "What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten. It should follow him to his grave."

Biden has harsh words for Donald Trump in his new memoir, "Promise Me, America," which goes on sale Nov. 17. He denounces Trump's decision to grant sweeping pardons and clemency to Jan. 6 defendants on his first day back in office and admonishes Trump for not holding a formal ceremony honoring the officers who defended the Capitol.

Early excerpts of the memoir were published Monday by The Atlantic.

Biden also reveals what happened inside the Oval Office during his nearly two-hour meeting with then President-elect Trump in November of 2024, describing a friendly tone from Trump that "bordered on fawning."

Trump defeated Kamala Harris to win the presidency after Biden withdrew from the race in July of 2024.

Oval Office meeting

Biden said he was taken aback by how warmly Trump greeted him just eight days after the bruising 2024 election. 

"Trump was immediately chatty and surprised me by adopting a tone so friendly that I thought he might be putting me on," Biden writes, adding that Trump told him, "You know, Joe, if it weren’t for politics, I believe we’d be good friends."

Biden said he was "too stunned to respond" and that Trump continued "as if intoxicated by the curious conversational path he had chosen."

"Yes, if it weren’t for politics, we’d spend all our time golfing together," Trump said, according to Biden.

Trump called Biden’s record on job creation "extraordinary" and, according to Biden, "relieved he didn’t have to run against me."

Biden said he cut off the compliments to move on to the business at hand, but as he gave a wide-ranging overview of issues that could define the Trump presidency, he noticed Trump was more focused on personalities of world leaders.

"As if we were sharing gossip about people at a dinner party, not discussing issues of global significance," Biden wrote.

Indictment of Trump’s second term

Biden said Trump’s "lies" have "kept coming" since taking office -- starting with the "utterly discredited claim that he had defeated me in 2020.”

"And they gained momentum as Trump took a wrecking ball to our traditions and institutions—at times literally, as when he tore down the East Wing of the White House (after promising that he would not)," Biden writes. The Electoral College certified Biden's victory in December of 2020.

Biden acknowledged that the policies of presidents are vulnerable to politics and can be undone at the whims of their successor, but argued "that feeling was magnified by the dismissive and destructive nature of Donald Trump.”

He said Trump "seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else’s accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down."

Biden took issue with Trump’s decision to again withdraw from the Paris climate accords, open public lands to drilling for oil, end support for electric vehicles and cancel wind and solar projects, making it harder for the U.S. to compete with China.

"Trump announced these policies at a rally as, at a five-star hotel across from the White House, oil and gas executives sipped champagne and nibbled on Pop-Tarts emblazoned with his image," he said.

He criticized DOGE as well as Trump’s decision to cut federal funding to Democratic states with no explanation, gut nonprofits and withdraw from the World Health Organization.

"It was clearly going to be a crueler government," Biden said.

"It was also going to be a government that stoked racial tensions instead of calming them," he added. "The new administration would launch a campaign to end the birthright-citizenship protections of the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution, a proud legacy of the Civil War. ICE officers would comb American cities, using expanded police powers to round up brown and Black people and detain them far from the courts and local police. We would be a less tolerant society, with raging conspiracy theories actively promoted by the White House and Trump’s constant and increasingly unhinged social-media feed."

Presidential immunity and the Supreme Court

Biden opened up about the 2024 Supreme Court decision that ruled presidents have some immunity from prosecution for acts that fall within their official duties.

"There was no precedent for that ruling," he said. "Common sense didn’t support it. There was no constitutional basis for it. It was inexplicable. Indefensible. And a death knell for accountability."

The former president warned that "no nation can survive character-free leadership for long" and that the U.S. is "no exception to that rule."
news.summary: Biden has harsh words for Donald Trump in his new memoir, "Promise Me, America," which goes on sale Nov. 17.
news.author: Justin Gomez,San Francisco

news.title: Stephen Miller’s promotion is ‘tone-deaf’ on what Americans want, CNN data analyst says
news.text:
CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten called Stephen Miller’s promotion to White House chief of staff “tone-deaf” following Republicans’ crushing midterm losses.

On Monday, Enten highlighted polling showing widespread opposition to President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, which Miller helped spearhead. Trump announced Friday that Miller, his deputy chief of staff, would replace Susie Wiles in the top job with his first day being Monday.

“Gosh, how tone-deaf is this White House?” Enten said. “You get the results from last week, and then you make Stephen Miller chief of staff? They’re in another planet, they’re in another universe.”

Enten, whom Trump has praised as the “best person on CNN,” pointed to sharp shifts toward Democrats in heavily Hispanic communities as evidence that Latino voters had soured on the administration.

“I mean, just look at these shifts,” he said. “Look at these shifts among Latino voters. And I got 'em across the political map for you.”

In Starr County, Texas, the vote shifted 72 percentage points toward Democrats between 2024 and 2026. Two other Hispanic communities — Passaic City, New Jersey, and Seward County, Kansas — recorded shifts of 54 and 52 points, respectively.

Enten also pointed to CNN survey data that showed Latino voters trusted Democrats more than Republicans on immigration by 21 points — compared to 2024, when they trusted Trump over Kamala Harris by 3 points.

Another CNN poll showed 68 percent of Latino voters — and 58 percent of voters overall — said the Trump administration’s immigration actions have gone too far.

“Latino support for Democrats, up like a rocket,” Enten said. “We saw it across the political map no matter what state, no matter what region you were in. And then…Donald Trump makes Stephen Miller chief of staff? What the heck is going on out there?”

Enten wasn’t the only political observer to question Trump’s elevation of Miller, a polarizing figure who helped shape some of the administration’s most controversial immigration initiatives, including its deportation crackdown and push to end birthright citizenship.

“Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote on X. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice.”

Even some Republicans have voiced concerns about the president’s decision.

“I think he's greatly hurt the administration and cost us many seats on Tuesday,” Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon told Fox News. “He took an immigration policy that favored the president 2:1 in the public, over-reached and made it 2:1 unfavorable.”

The White House previously told The Independent that Miller has played a central role in the president’s policies.

“Stephen Miller has been a key player in delivering on President Trump’s America First agenda since day one,” spokesperson Lauren Bis said. “He has spearheaded the administration’s crime crackdown including in D.C. and Memphis, record setting deregulation, unleashed American energy, dismantled drug cartels, and secured our border. In his new role, he will continue to deliver historic successes for the American people.”

news.title: Cancer treatment prompts Biden to reduce memoir promotion
news.text:
Former US president Joe Biden says he is scaling back plans to promote his upcoming memoir as he undergoes treatment for aggressive prostate cancer, acknowledging that the illness sometimes leaves him struggling.

The 83-year-old Democrat, whose cognitive decline was a major issue during his presidency and ultimately ended his bid to stay in power, has said that he would be unable to make as many public appearances as he had hoped ahead of the 17 November release of "Promise Me, America."

"Some days are better than others. It hasn't stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down," Mr Biden wrote on X.

"What that means is, unfortunately, I won't be able to do as many conversations about my book as I'd hoped. However, I'm hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves."

Mr Biden announced in May 2025, four months after leaving the White House, that he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that had spread to his bones.

He has since undergone radiation and hormone therapy, while his son Hunter said in August that the disease had spread further and was causing considerable pain.

Mr Biden struck an optimistic note about his treatment, saying his doctors "continue to be encouraged" by his response.

His memoir chronicles his four years in the White House, including his handling of the Covid-19 pandemic, his widely criticised withdrawl from Afghanistan, Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and his controversial decision to seek reelection in 2024 before withdrawing, a move some Democrats said handed the presidency to Donald Trump.

In an excerpt published by The Atlantic, Biden complained about his successor over the 2021 assault on the US Capitol.

"What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten. It should follow him to his grave," Mr Biden wrote.

He also recalled an unexpectedly friendly Oval Office meeting with President Trump following the Republican's 2024 election victory, during which his successor suggested they might have been friends outside politics.

Mr Biden abandoned his reelection campaign in July 2024 after a disastrous debate against Mr Trump intensified concerns about his age, mental capacity and fitness for office.

His vice president, Kamala Harris, subsequently lost the election, returning Mr Trump to the White House.

Mr Biden said his book would explain the decisions he made in office and reflect his faith in American democracy.

news.title: Biden, in White House memoir, says Trump should carry the weight of Jan. 6 riots 'to his grave'
news.text: Former President Biden writes in his White House memoir that Donald Trump, at once his predecessor and successor, has deeply damaged the country and world with an administration determined to “tear down institutions and inflame hatreds.” And the 83-year-old Democrat said the 80-year-old Trump's years of lies about his 2020 defeat to Biden and the Jan. 6 attacks on the Capitol should “follow him to his grave.” Biden's sweeping indictment comes in the first excerpt of “Promise Me, America,” published Monday by the Atlantic. The 46th president's full memoir is set for a Nov. 17 release. Biden said that while doctors are encouraged by his response to cancer treatment, his activities promoting the book will be limited because of his health. “Donald Trump led an insurrection," Biden wrote of the attack by Trump supporters as Congress met to certify the 2020 election won by the Democrat. "His goal was to remain in power after the American people had voted him out of office. “The rioters weren’t ‘peaceful protesters," he wrote. “They came armed to stop the official certification of a legitimate election.” He chided Trump for later issuing more than 1,500 pardons of the offenders. “To this day, Trump and his supporters continue to preen and posture like they’re supporters of law enforcement,” Biden wrote. “Here’s my view: You don’t get to turn a blind eye to cops being punched, speared, sprayed, and brutalized and call yourself a friend of law enforcement. What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten. It should follow him to his grave.” Biden also laments Trump's Department of Government Efficiency and his aggressive reversal of many of his policies, especially those intended to address climate change. “All presidents must confront a feeling that their legacy is vulnerable to the pendulum of politics and the whims of their successors,” Biden wrote. “In my case, that feeling was magnified by the dismissive and destructive nature of Donald Trump, who seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else’s accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down.” The memoir's release comes on the heels of Biden's fellow Democrats trouncing Republicans in the midterm elections, securing stunningly broad House and Senate majorities and flipping control of several statehouses in a comprehensive rebuke of Trump's second presidency. But Trump's return to power two years earlier was itself a rejection of Biden's one White House term, and many voters still harbor skeptical views of his presidency and his party. In a lengthy social media post on Sunday, Biden pitched his memoir as the best way he can explain his presidency, “the challenges we faced, the decisions I made and why I made them.” During his four years in office, Biden confronted the COVID-19 pandemic and its economic fallout, and he worked to restore global alliances that Trump frayed. But he faced widespread concerns about his age, and he abandoned his reelection bid after a disastrous June 2024 debate with Trump. Dogged by lingering inflation and other concerns, Biden’s vice president, Kamala Harris, lost to Trump that November. Months after leaving office, Biden announced that he'd been diagnosed with prostate cancer. He opened up about his condition in his Sunday social media post, saying he “won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped” and urging people to let the book speak for him. Biden said his doctors “continue to be encouraged by how I've responded to treatment.” But, he acknowledged, “Some days are better than others. It hasn't stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.” In the excerpt, Biden recounts an unusual Oval Office meeting with Trump days after the 2020 election — well before the Jan. 6 riots. “‘You know, Joe, if it weren't for politics, I believe we'd be good friends,’” Trump said, according to Biden. Trump even commented "that he’d been relieved he didn’t have to run against me," Biden added. Public polling at the time Biden dropped his reelection bid showed him trailing Trump, and Democrats pushed for him to yield out of fear that he could not win. Biden said he used the meeting to give Trump “a tour of the world,” including the Ukraine-Russia war, NATO alliances, Israel and Gaza and China-U.S. relations. Biden said Trump “focused on the personalities” of world leaders rather than the substance of international relations. He said that two-hour meeting left him worried Trump would indeed dismantle much of his presidency. He wrote that Trump's opening weeks — his Day One executive orders and everything that followed — confirmed his worries about a “crueler government” that “tried to tear down institutions and inflame hatreds” and a president who “took a wrecking ball to our traditions.” The memoir's title echoes an earlier Biden book, “Promise Me, Dad,” that he wrote about his son Beau's cancer and death — a parallel that implicitly acknowledges the former president's age, condition and the reality that he may not have a long post-presidency to see the direction of the country and the evolution of his legacy. In that first book, released between Biden's vice presidency and his 2020 presidential bid, he explained that the title came directly from a father-son conversation around Thanksgiving in 2014. “Promise me, Dad. Give me your word that no matter what happens, you’re going to be all right,” Biden recalled Beau saying. Beau Biden died six months later. In his Sunday post, Biden repeated an argument he made often when campaigning and during his presidency, saying the U.S. is unique because it was “built on an idea” that “all of us are created equal.” “Promise me, America,” he concluded, that “we'll never forget it.” Barrow writes for the Associated Press.
